title: Lawsuits allege that ignored warnings led to deadly Brooklyn building collapse
description:
NEW YORK (AP) — As investigators probe what caused a New York City building collapse that killed eight people, workers and residents are painting a portrait of two trouble spots side-by-side: the apartment house that fell down and the construction site being excavated next door.
Lawsuits filed since the Nov. 11 disaster in Brooklyn cast blame in multiple directions: at the construction site owner and contractors; at an engineering firm that drew up the excavation plan; and at the owner of the building that collapsed. Several injured workers have also taken steps toward suing the city agency that polices construction safety.
A key question for investigators is whether work underway to dig a deep pit for a new building undermined the foundation of the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave., causing it to topple into the jobsite.
A lawsuit filed by five injured construction workers said the dig at 2625 Bedford Ave. lacked adequate retaining walls, shoring and underpinning to keep the adjoining building safe, and that excavation work continued even after the building's facade began to crack.
“The shoring that they were planning to keep the collapsed building up was severely insufficient,” said lawyer Jonathan Damashek, who has sued on behalf of injured workers. He questioned whether the city should have approved the plans, and whether contractors' work was negligent.
Damashek’s lawsuits accuse defendants, including construction manager Townhouse Homes, of failing “to consider public safety above their own concern of keeping down costs.”
The litigation comes as families mourn the dead — among them two children. City officials said Wednesday that another building adjoining the one that crumbled will have to be demolished after the collapse peeled off an outer wall.
Tenant says construction work next door led to cracks
Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani vowed to do “everything we can to understand exactly how this collapse occurred, so that the responsible parties can be held to account.” His department is hiring an independent engineering consultant to help. Brooklyn prosecutors also are investigating.
The Buildings Department said by email Friday that it reviewed the excavation and support plans and found they complied with city requirements. As for examining what actually got installed, the agency noted that the city requires private inspectors — hired by developers — to check some stages of construction. 
The agency didn't answer a question about whether it responded to a preconstruction survey that found the adjoining wall of the now-collapsed building “in poor condition with noticeable cracks.”
That three-story brick structure, erected nearly a century ago, had its own woes — over 90 unresolved citations for exposed wiring, roof leaks, faulty doors and other alleged housing code violations.
Conditions worsened once construction ramped up next door, tenant Dengane Omari Jack said in a lawsuit.
Jack, who lost his extensive record collection and other personal effects, said he was rebuffed when he tried warning the landlord about cracks he noticed near the building’s entrance. After providing photos of the damage, Jack was told it wasn’t the landlord’s fault and couldn’t be fixed, the lawsuit said.
Builder and excavation engineer have faced lawsuits
While the investigation proceeds, the city is checking out over 160 construction sites tied to companies involved in the project at 2625 Bedford Ave., a planned apartment and commercial building.
Townhouse, which also operates as Promont, has been heavily involved in New York’s construction scene over the last three decades.
In 2016, it was accused in lawsuits of damaging an adjacent building during a Manhattan renovation project, which it denied, and compromising the structural integrity of adjacent structures while performing excavation, pile driving and steel beam installation for a Brooklyn hotel. The company's lawyers haven't addressed the allegations in the lawsuit involving the hotel.
Principals in Townhouse, other firms named in this report and the property owners haven’t responded to The Associated Press’ requests for comment. 
The Bedford Avenue project’s excavation engineer, Jieming Wang, has also faced lawsuits. At least a dozen have blamed excavation plans designed by his firm, New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group, for damage at adjacent properties, court records show.
A 2015 lawsuit alleged that LMW’s work on a Manhattan excavation site caused sloping floors, damaged doors and windows and destroyed utility pipes at an adjacent building.
In 2016, the wall of a building next to a Queens excavation project was undermined by soil removal, another lawsuit said. A 2020 lawsuit accused the firm of skipping required testing and monitoring at another Queens project. A neighboring building’s foundation was left unstable, its gas and hot water systems were damaged and an architectural arch partially separated from the structure, the lawsuit said.
The company, which has worked on bridges, airports and other projects since its 1998 founding, denied the allegations in the 2015 and 2016 cases but hasn't responded to the 2020 lawsuit. Other litigation was resolved out of court.
City fined project during demolition phase
The Bedford Avenue project ran afoul of the Buildings Department in March for starting to demolish an existing structure without installing enough netting and other protections from flying debris.
Demolition contractor N Tech Design of America was ordered to stop the work — but continued, got caught again in April, admitted both violations and paid a total of $12,500 in fines, city records show.
N Tech representative Aramis Brown told local news outlet The City Reporter that the company finished its work at the site in May and had nothing to do with the excavation or the collapse.
The excavation work started, with city permission, in September.
Collapsed building owner was on “worst landlords” list
The owner of the building that collapsed, Olufemi Falade, has held a slate of Brooklyn buildings under various corporate names — and has been listed on the city public advocate's “100 worst landlords” roster six times in the last decade. 
Falade, a licensed professional engineer, was jailed for 12 days in 2006 for failing to fix violations in a dozen buildings. Then-Housing Commissioner Shaun Donovan called him “one of the most egregious examples we’ve seen citywide of flouting the law and forcing his residents to live in horrible conditions.”
Falade told the Village Voice after his release that tenants weren't paying rent. “People want something for nothing,” he fumed.
He hasn't responded to the AP's requests for comment since the collapse.
At a vigil near the collapse site on Wednesday, housing activists, faith leaders and others called for Falade and the developers to be held accountable.
“New housing cannot come at the expense of tenants’ lives,” said Judith Douglas, a tenant advocate who lives in Flatbush.
This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/lawsuits-allege-corner-cutting-ignored-203044293.html

title: Bitcoin Poised For 'Great' 2027 as Fed Eyes Aggressive Rate Cuts, Expert Says
description:
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) could stage a strong recovery in 2027 as the Federal Reserve shifts from near-term tightening to aggressive monetary easing.
Speaking in an interview with Bitcoin Magazine, “42 Macro” founder and CEO Darius Dale said the Fed’s expected December rate hike does not constitute a policy mistake because the U.S. economy remains exceptionally strong.
He expects a potential Fed-Treasury coordination framework to support long-term Treasury markets and improve liquidity conditions.
“We think that surprising and dramatic easing in 2027 and beyond is still on the table,” Dale said.
Worsening liquidity conditions, persistent inflation and risks surrounding AI infrastructure spending could trigger another market selloff before Bitcoin establishes a bottom.
Dale predicts 2027 should be a great year for Bitcoin, with easier monetary policy potentially supporting cryptocurrencies, gold, silver and equities.
Why Is Bitcoin Falling Ahead of Other Assets?
Dale said Bitcoin signals weakening liquidity before gold and equities because its volatility makes it more sensitive to tightening financial conditions.
He expects Bitcoin to bottom ahead of other assets within months, with inflation easing by the second quarter of 2027.
However, year-end de-risking, AI infrastructure uncertainty and institutional selling could extend the downturn, echoing late 2018.
Bitcoin’s Bullish 2027 Outlook
Dale expects AI-driven productivity gains to boost economic growth, corporate profits and asset valuations in 2027.
Growing institutional adoption could reduce Bitcoin’s volatility, limiting both sharp crashes and explosive rallies.
He emphasized managing risk over predicting market bottoms, noting his firm’s risk management models had previously signaled Bitcoin exits.

title: SEC Charges Eight Firms in $37M Crypto Scam Using Fake Trading Platforms
description: The US Securities and Exchange Commission SEC charges eight Colorado-based entities accused of defrauding American investors of more than $37 million through fake investment advisory services and cryptocurrency trading platforms. According to the regulator, the alleged scheme relied on social media advertisements, private messaging groups and fabricated regulatory documents to convince victims they were dealing […]
fullContent:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission SEC charges eight Colorado-based entities accused of defrauding American investors of more than $37 million through fake investment advisory services and cryptocurrency trading platforms.

According to the regulator, the alleged scheme relied on social media advertisements, private messaging groups and fabricated regulatory documents to convince victims they were dealing with legitimate financial professionals. Investors were initially offered stock market advice before being directed to platforms that appeared to facilitate cryptocurrency purchases but were allegedly created to steal their money.

The SEC believes individuals operating from overseas were likely behind the operation, which ran from August 2024 through May 2026. Rather than relying on a single company identity, the alleged perpetrators moved through four successive combinations of investment advisers and crypto platforms, abandoning each setup after several months.

The case highlights how scammers continue to exploit the growing interest in digital assets by using the appearance of regulatory approval and professional investment services to gain victims’ trust.

Fake Investment Advisers Used Social Media to Target Investors

The SEC’s complaint describes a process that began with advertisements on social media platforms. These promotions directed potential investors into group chats and private conversations controlled by individuals allegedly involved in the fraud.

People participating in the chats presented themselves as representatives of investment advisory businesses and initially provided guidance on trading US stocks. Once investors developed confidence in the supposed advisers, they were encouraged to transfer larger amounts of money to cryptocurrency trading platforms.

Victims were led to believe that they were purchasing genuine digital assets through these services. However, the SEC alleges that the platforms were fraudulent fronts intended to collect investor funds rather than facilitate legitimate cryptocurrency transactions.

The operators also allegedly used fabricated SEC certificates and misleading regulatory records to make their businesses appear authentic. Some investors who questioned the legitimacy of the services were directed to filings submitted to the SEC, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

Eight Entities Named in the SEC Complaint

The SEC identified eight Colorado-based entities involved in the alleged operation:

  • Advisor WeChat Capital

  • Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance Ltd.

  • HB Wealth Advisors

  • IdeaCrypto Exchange LLC

  • Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc.

  • RealSimple Crypto Exchange Inc.

  • Associated Wealth Advisors Ltd.

  • Essential Crypto Exchange

According to the complaint, the entities operated through four successive adviser-and-platform pairings between August 2024 and May 2026. The alleged perpetrators switched to new business identities every few months, allowing the scheme to continue under different names.

The regulator is seeking permanent injunctions, conduct-based restrictions, repayment of allegedly ill-gotten gains, prejudgment interest and civil penalties. The charges remain allegations, and the defendants have not been established as liable through a final court judgment.

SEC Warns Investors About Crypto Scams and Fake Regulatory Credentials

The latest case follows previous SEC warnings about investment fraud schemes promoted through messaging applications and online group chats.

In December 2025, the regulator issued an investor alert highlighting how scammers impersonate financial professionals and use group conversations to promote fraudulent investment opportunities. The agency has also warned that claims of SEC registration should not be treated as proof that an investment or platform is legitimate.

The SEC encourages investors to check the background of individuals and businesses offering financial products through its Investor.gov resources. It also recommends reporting suspected investment fraud through the agency’s online reporting portal.

While those figures cover different reporting periods, they provide context for the regulator’s recent enforcement activity involving digital assets.

The SEC’s latest action underscores how fraudulent operators can exploit the reputation of established financial institutions and regulatory agencies to make fake crypto services appear credible. For investors, verifying the identity and registration status of an adviser or platform remains an important step before transferring funds.

title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on tech companies that build AI centers overseas
description:
President Trump on Friday threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on U.S. tech companies if they build data centers in other countries. 
"We're gonna fight very hard for the data centers," he said at a press conference Friday morning. "We're not gonna allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country."
The president did not provide any specifics on how the tax plan might work and told reporters that he hadn't even informed members of his own administration of his intention to implement it. 
Trump has been a persistent advocate of data center construction throughout his second term, calling the facilities a "Golden Goose" for the U.S. economy. That stance puts him at odds with the views of most Americans. Recent polls show that a strong majority of those surveyed oppose a new data center being built in their communities, while only a small percentage strongly support the idea. Even Republican voters are largely against data centers.  
A few years ago, the typical American hardly ever thought about data centers. But they've become a major political issue seemingly overnight. We've seen local lawmakers lose their jobs over their support for new data center projects. Debates over the facilities were also a key pivot point in the midterm elections earlier this month, with exit polls showing that strong majorities of voters opposed having one built in their communities.  
Lawmakers from both parties have responded to the dramatic shift against data centers by ramping up efforts to slow down, or even block entirely, data center construction. In July, New York became the first state to ban new data center projects. Similar proposals have been put forward in more than a dozen other states. 
There has also been momentum in Congress behind plans to rein in data centers nationwide. One of those proposals, the Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA), passed through the House in a near-unanimous vote in September, but has been stalled in the Senate ever since. 
The RPA would compel state utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard under which large data centers would cover the extra costs of upgrades. Several senators have pushed for separate legislation that represents much more aggressive efforts to curb data center-related utility costs. That includes a proposed bill that would empower federal regulators to force tech companies to cover certain costs that come from connecting their data centers to the grid. 
A separate bipartisan bill, the GRID Act, would go even further by requiring all new data centers to have their own independent power supply that's completely separate from the public grid. Progressive lawmakers Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have called for a full, nationwide moratorium on new data centers "until strong national safeguards are in place." 
All this is happening at a time when the president and the country's biggest tech companies are saying that the U.S. needs to dramatically increase its data capacity in order to build the economy of the future. 
With that in mind, here are answers to some of the most important questions you may have about data centers, including why we need them, why thousands more are being built and what it means for local communities when a new data center comes to town.  
What are data centers?
Data centers are often called the "physical infrastructure of the internet." They are facilities where the servers, networking equipment and storage systems that allow digital data to be processed, stored and transmitted are housed. 
Why do we need data centers?
At a fundamental level, the modern internet simply cannot exist without them. Every email, social media post, video or news article that you can find online runs through a data center. 
How many data centers are there?
There are an estimated 3,000 data centers currently operating across the United States, according to a Pew analysis of industry data published in April. The facilities aren't evenly distributed, though. Virginia has nearly 400, while data centers in some states number in the single digits. 
How many more are being built?
There are roughly 1,500 new data centers in "various stages of development" nationwide, according to Pew. Other estimates suggest there could be as many as 3,000. But that doesn't just mean more of the same types of facilities that already exist are being built. Some of the proposed data centers are much larger than anything that's currently in operation. According to the power market tracking company Clearview, the biggest active data center in the U.S. has a power capacity of 750 megawatts. A single data center that's been proposed in Utah would have an estimated capacity of nearly 9,000 megawatts. 
Data centers aren't just getting bigger. They're also being built in new places. Right now, the vast majority of active data centers are in urban areas, according to Pew. More than two-thirds of the incoming data centers will be in rural areas. 



Why do we need so many more data centers?
The more we ask the internet to do, the more computing power is needed to meet our demands. 
Over the course of the past two decades, the U.S. has had to steadily build more and more data centers as so many aspects of our lives have moved online. But the recent, dramatic increase in data center projects isn't being driven by the spread of social media, the rise of streaming or the remote work revolution. It's being driven by AI.
AI works by processing huge data sets to learn, adapt and make predictions in a way that typical algorithms can't. That takes a lot of processing power. The kind of processing power that America's data infrastructure simply won't be able to handle as AI becomes more complex and widespread, without a massive increase in data center capacity. 
Tech companies are pouring money into building more data centers to support their lofty AI ambitions, which many see as a world-changing technology that will be at the core of everything we do. One estimate found that it could take $6.7 trillion in global data center investment before the end of the decade to create the scale of computing power that's needed to support AI's continued growth. 
How have opinions on data centers changed?
Data centers have been around in some form as long as computers have. Until recently, most Americans had no real strong opinion about them, if they were aware of their existence at all. But public opinion has shifted dramatically against data centers over a remarkably short period of time, as people across the country are being faced with the prospect of having one built in their back communities. 
The share of Americans who say they would strongly oppose a new data center near where they live more than doubled, growing from 24% to 55%, in the span of just nine months, according to a June poll by Heatmap. Other surveys have shown that a strong majority of Americans do not want data centers built in their communities. 
Anti-data center sentiment has been especially intense in areas where they're being built. There's a growing list of local lawmakers who have been voted out after approving the construction of new facilities. A recent study tracked the creation of hundreds of new local Facebook groups with more than 400,000 total members dedicated to bringing residents together in opposition to proposed data centers in their communities.
Why have data centers become so controversial?
There are many reasons people cite for why they oppose data centers. The most prominent concerns center around the amount of resources the facilities consume. Data centers use up a ton of electricity and need a lot of water to keep all those servers from overheating. 
New facilities are also massive construction projects, which bring all sorts of disruptions to communities while they're being built — road closures, construction noise, huge trucks clogging up streets and more. 
Many data center critics say it's just unpleasant to live near one. One of the main complaints is noise, which some residents have described as like having a "freight train" constantly running past their homes. Researchers have found that large data centers can have a "heat island" effect that makes the surrounding area noticeably hotter. 
Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest against AI data center expansion in Imperial, California on July 18, 2026.
SANDY HUFFAKER via Getty Images

Broader skepticism of AI is also a big factor. Tech companies have argued that the U.S. needs to build all of these new data centers to support their vision of an AI-powered future. But more Americans say they expect AI to have a negative impact on society when you account for how it will affect the labor market, education, environment and our personal relationships. It's a tough sell to ask people to tolerate the downsides of having a data center in their community when they don't want the products that the facilities are being built to support.
Finally, there's the phenomenon commonly known as NIMBYism. The acronym, which stands for Not In My Back Yard, is often used derisively to describe people who say they support the construction of things our society needs — affordable housing, power plants, prisons and public transportation — but refuse to accept those things being built where they live. In the eyes of some proponents of data centers, local opposition to building them is a classic case of NIMBYism in action. 
How much power do they use?
A lot. In 2024, data centers accounted for 4% of all power consumption in the United States. With so many facilities being built, the total amount of electricity data centers consume is projected to more than double by 2030, according to estimates from the International Energy Agency. A separate study estimated that data centers could account for up to 12% of all power usage in the U.S. by 2028. 
A typical newly built "hyperscale" facility can require as much power as 100,000 households. The largest data centers can consume more energy than entire major cities, and demand is higher in places with the most facilities. In Virginia, for example, data centers consumed 40% of the state's electricity in 2024, according to a Bloomberg analysis. 
Utility companies have also spent billions building out transmission lines and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the local power grid and building new power plants to meet increased demand. 
How do they affect utility rates?
It's important to note that all of the tangible information we have on data centers and energy prices is based on what's already been built. At this point, experts can only estimate what will happen when all of those new proposed facilities eventually begin operating. 
That said, there's already evidence that the data centers that are currently online have had an impact on electricity rates, thanks to a combination of higher operational costs for utilities and increased demand. 
Residential power rates have roughly doubled over the past 10 years. How much data centers are to blame for that increase is the source of significant debate. Some recent analyses have found that states with the most data centers have seen their energy rates climb at a faster rate than the national average. But another study suggested that their impact on electricity bills has been modest — at least so far.
Some in the energy and tech industries even argue that data centers can actually lower energy prices. While there's some evidence to support that claim in certain areas, most experts believe the large-scale buildout of data centers across the country will push prices higher in the long run. 
A variety of solutions have been proposed to keep that from happening, including forcing data center companies to pay for any new infrastructure or plants that utilities have to build to power them, charging the centers higher rates than typical consumers and even requiring data centers to have their own on-site power plants.  
An aerial view of the Stargate Oracle AI data center campus in Abilene, Texas.
Brandon Bell via Getty Images

How much water do they consume?
Data centers use water to keep the thousands of servers and other equipment they house from overheating. One estimate found that the typical non-hyperscale data center uses about 300,000 gallons of water per day, about as much as 1,000 U.S. households. Newer, larger facilities can use as much as 5 million gallons every day. 
In total, data centers used up an estimated 66 billion gallons of water in 2023, according to an analysis by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That same study estimated that data center water demand could double by 2028.
While that is a lot of water, it's a relatively small share of the 117 trillion gallons the United States uses every year, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. 
There are also ways to significantly reduce the amount of water data centers use. Historically, most data centers relied on what's known as an open-loop cooling system, in which water is brought in, then evaporated to cool the air around servers. While that's the cheapest way to prevent servers from overheating, it's also very inefficient. There are other, closed-loop approaches that allow facilities to reuse water, which can cut a data center's water demand by up to 70%.
More than half of all global data centers still rely on open-loop systems, but some of the biggest companies in the tech industry, including OpenAI, have said they plan to prioritize closed-loop facilities moving forward.  
That change only addresses the water that data centers use directly. The facilities also impact water supplies in a larger way through their electricity consumption. The vast majority of power plants in the U.S. use water to keep their own systems from overheating. As a result, the extra strain that data centers put on electricity providers accounts for an additional 800 billion gallons of water consumed annually, according to Lawrence Berkeley Lab. 
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has tried to appease concerns about water usage, telling the Sources Podcast in September that data centers use no more water than an office building and that 38,000 ChatGPT queries use as much water as the production of one almond. It's a claim that many experts feel is difficult to verify given the limited amount of public information made available by AI companies and the number of vairables at play when trying to acuurately analyze each data center's water usage.
How many jobs do they create?
Like any major construction project, a new data center creates a lot of short-term jobs while it's being built. But once it's completed and operational, the facilities take a relatively small number of people to keep them running. The average data center creates between 100 and 200 permanent full-time jobs locally, according to a recent study by the Brookings Institution. 
Of course, data centers don't only affect employment at the local level. The entire U.S. economy relies on the existence of infrastructure that allows us to consistently and reliably send information over the internet. At a very basic level, we need data centers. The questions of how many we need, where they should go and who should bear the costs are where the real debate lies.

title: Fiona the hippo's necropsy shows why supportive care couldn't save her
description:
A necropsy has revealed that the knit cap responsible for the death of the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo Fiona was lodged so deep in her digestive tract that she effectively had no chance of survival. 
Zoo officials said on Friday that the hat got stuck 25 feet beyond Fiona's final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines.
"Upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object," explained Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health. "The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."
Weinninger added that the zoo's other hippos, Tucker and Fritz, along with Fiona's mother, Bibi, "are eating and behaving normally. It's difficult to know how they're feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves."
"Keepers, vets, staff, and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss," Wenninger said. "She meant a lot to a lot of people."

It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency. https://t.co/X0GVbDAiEQ pic.twitter.com/7wLF0uclWB
— Cincinnati Zoo (@CincinnatiZoo) November 19, 2026
The zoo announced Fiona's death on Thursday, 11 days after she swallowed a hat that had slipped into her enclosure.  She was nine years old.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said in a statement.
Fans near and far have been grieving ever since. Thayne Maynard, executive chair of the zoo's board, compared Fiona to "lightning in a bottle," adding that he had "never known an animal so beloved in all my life."
On Friday, zoo visitors draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon, according to the Associated Press. A young girl held up a drawing of Fiona; someone else left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona's favorite treats.
Flowers, handwritten notes, watermelons and other items are displayed at a memorial for Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo.
AP Photo/Obed Lamy
Flowers and cards rest by a statue outside the Cincinnati Zoo.
AP Photo/Sallee Ann Harrison

"They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don't regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does," Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, told the Associated Press. "Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid and digesting food easily 'hide' the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult." 
Hippos are also difficult to anesthetize and keep away from water as they heal. 
Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told reporters that Fiona ingested the knit hat on Nov. 8 after it was tossed in the air by a child and flung by a ceiling fan through a 1-foot opening above the viewing windows of her enclosure. "We probably couldn't make that happen again if we tried," Curley said at the time. "It was clearly an accident."

"Our city is heartbroken," Mayor Aftab Pureval wrote on social media, "but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."
"Our hearts are with the staff of the Cincinnati Zoo and everyone who loved her," added outgoing Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine. "She will be deeply missed."
Amy Acton, Ohio's incoming governor, said that Fiona's survival story "brought joy, hope and a little extra magic to our state."
On Friday, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno introduced a resolution honoring Fiona and the Cincinnati Zoo staff on the floor of the U.S. Senate. It passed unanimously.

— Bernie Moreno (@berniemoreno) November 20, 2026
"Fiona was a symbol of resilience, of perseverance, and we're going to miss her in Cincinnati," Moreno said. Her loss, he added, will "leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in the heart."

title: S&P 500 Drops Below 7,000 as Nvidia Faces Accounting Investigation
description:
The S&P 500 broke below 7,000 as Nvidia's SEC probe reportedly turned to accounting. See the next market triggers.
The post S&P 500 Drops Below 7,000 as Nvidia Faces Accounting Investigation appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
S&P 500 has dropped 3% on Friday, dropping below 7,000 to its lowest price in 6 months. This comes as reports suggest the SEC is investigating Nvidia’s accounting. 

Meanwhile, Nvidia shares fell 12% to $128 – its lowest price in over a year. NVDA reportedly accounts for 6.1% of the  S&P 500

SEC Probe Into Nvidia’s Accounting

The Wall Street Journal first reported the civil probe on Nov. 17. Its focus then was whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors.

Friday’s reports said the inquiry now explores potential accounting issues. The SEC has not confirmed the probe or named the items under review.

The executive running Nvidia has overseen its finances since 2013.

Colette Kress became interim CEO on Nov. 11 after Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia’s filing said she would keep the CFO role.

One reporting change has drawn scrutiny. Nvidia stopped listing Singapore as a separate revenue region in late 2025, after it billed $10.2 billion there in one quarter.

Nvidia said it switched to grouping sales by customer headquarters.

The Next Market Triggers for Nvidia and the S&P 500

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent gave Nvidia’s board and outside counsel 10 days to answer questions. He asked whether Nvidia knowingly sold chips to China to lift earnings.

On Dec. 1, Huang faces closed-door interviews with three House committees. General counsel Tim Teter follows on Dec. 2.

Nvidia also held back its quarterly report, the 10-Q, after Tuesday’s earnings. The 40-day filing window from the Oct. 25 quarter end closes in early December.

Nvidia has settled with the SEC before. In 2022, it paid $5.5 million over undisclosed crypto mining sales.

Nvidia now trades about 46% below its 52-week high of $243.37. Its slide sits inside a wider AI and tech selloff that also hit AMD this week.

title: Zcash Price Crashes Through $800 With Little Support Below
description:
Key Takeaways Mid-November support near $800 gave way. Bounce stalled at the 0.5 level near $975. 50-day average falling fast […]
The post Zcash Price Crashes Through $800 With Little Support Below appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Mid-November support near $800 gave way.
  • Bounce stalled at the 0.5 level near $975.
  • 50-day average falling fast toward the 100-day.
  • RSI just under 30, no capitulation volume.

Friday’s drop came as part of a broader selloff across the crypto market.

A 15% Candle Through the $800-$810 Zone

ZEC opened Friday near $894, reached $899 and then fell as low as $746. As of 19:36 UTC, with more than four hours left in the session, it traded near $763, down 14.67%. That puts price under two levels that sit almost on top of each other: the 200-day simple moving average at $810 and the 0.618 retracement near $800.

The zone had already been tested once. ZEC’s first leg down in mid-November stopped just above it, and buyers pushed price back up from there. When ZEC traded near $921 earlier this week, Coindoo’s weekly chart analysis named the 200-day as the nearest daily support if the weekly channel floor gave way. On Friday the candle went straight through it, taking ZEC to prices it last traded at in late August.

How the Decline Built

From the peak to Friday, one step down at a time
Late September
Peak near $1,700
Early October
Rising trendline from the June low gives way
Oct – early Nov
Range capped around the 0.236 level near $1,355, with wicks above it but closes below
Mid-November
Range floor breaks; first slide stops just above $800-$810
Earlier this week
Bounce stalls at the 0.5 level near $975
November 20
Candle cuts through $800–$810

Each support has also held for less time than the one before. The October range kept ZEC up for about five weeks. The mid-November low lasted about one.

Little Trading History Below $746

Friday’s low near $746 marks the bottom of the area where ZEC paused after its August breakout. Below it, the climb from about $550 to $800 happened so fast that the chart has almost no closes in between. That’s why the next labeled support sits as far down as the 0.786 retracement near $560.

Trading history between $450 and $900
▼ -$763
$450
$900
■ $450–$500: core of the summer base, about two months of trading
■ $500–$580: upper summer range, with its ceiling near $560 tested in July
■ $580–$746: crossed in a few late-August candles
■ $746–$900: about two weeks of trading in late August and early September

Averages Overhead, Momentum Just Turning Oversold

ZEC has now lost all three daily averages, one at a time: the 50-day in October, the 100-day in the mid-November break and the 200-day, at $810, on Friday. Higher up, the 50-day at $1,169 is falling fast toward the 100-day at $1,116, which is still rising but flattening. The 0.382 retracement near $1,145 sits between the two, which makes $1,116-$1,169 the densest resistance band on the chart. The 50-day is still above the 100-day, but the gap between them has narrowed sharply since early November.

The 14-day RSI reads 29.52, just under the 30 line that marks oversold territory and well below its own average at 37.01. It has only just crossed that threshold: a fresh oversold reading, not a deep one.

Volume reads 238.25K ZEC with more than four hours left in the session, small next to the spikes that marked the June low and the late-August breakout. Nothing on the chart yet resembles the volume of a washout.

What the Daily Close Sets Up

BREAKDOWN HOLDS
Below $800
If: ZEC closes below $800 and retests into the $800-$825 zone fail
Then: the broken 200-day becomes resistance, and the $560–$580 area, just above the 0.786 level, is the next reference
WASHOUT AND BASE
Near $560
If: price reaches the area near $560 or sweeps into $500-$540, with a volume spike and RSI steadying in the low 20s
Then: the chart would show the exhaustion this week’s selling has lacked, at the strongest support below $746. If $560 gives way, the $450–$500 base is the next reference
FAILED BREAKDOWN
Above $860
If: ZEC closes back above $825-$850, reclaiming both the 200-day and the 0.618 level, and then clears $860
Then: Friday’s drop becomes a failed breakdown, and the 0.5 level near $975 comes back into range

That leaves ZEC with resistance about 6% above, at the 200-day average, and the next labeled support about 27% below, near $560.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not financial, investment or trading advice. The levels and scenarios describe chart conditions, not price predictions. Cryptocurrencies are highly volatile; do your own research before making any decision.

title: The next Senate has 98 names. 2 incoming governors can fill in the final blanks.
description:
The last undecided Senate race finally got a winner on Tuesday night when Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to give her party its ninth flipped seat this midterm cycle. 
Peltola’s win, which came more than two weeks after Election Day, means the final balance of power in the Senate is set. When the new Congress convenes for the first time in January, Democrats will control 56 seats, and Republicans will hold 44 seats. 
But there are still two important questions that remain unanswered about the next Senate caucus. As it stands, we only know the identities of 98 of the 100 senators who will serve in the upcoming Congress, and it could be weeks before we find out who those last two pivotal lawmakers will be. 
That’s because two current senators, Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn and Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar, were each elected governor of their home states. They will need to leave the Senate to assume their new positions. 
Laws in Tennessee and Minnesota give governors the power to temporarily fill Senate vacancies. That means Blackburn and Klobuchar can each choose their own successor as one of their first acts as governor if they wait to resign from the Senate until shortly before they’re sworn in. Both have indicated they plan to do so but have offered very few clues about who they might consider. 
It’s highly unlikely that either of them would select a replacement from the opposition party, so the partisan split in the Senate probably won’t change. But their decisions will still carry a lot of weight. Whoever they choose will occupy two of the most important legislative seats in the U.S. government and could play a significant role in defining the ideological direction of their respective parties. 
Volunteers in Tennessee
Blackburn, who has represented Tennessee in the Senate since 2019, announced her bid for governor in August 2025, just nine months after winning reelection to a second Senate term. This year’s gubernatorial race was much closer than Republicans in the Volunteer State are accustomed to, but Blackburn was still able to defeat her Democratic challenger, Jerri Green, by more than 50,000 votes. She is the first woman elected to the state’s top office. 
Blackburn is a staunch conservative and Trump ally. She opened her first gubernatorial campaign video by saying, “Trump is back. America is blessed and Tennessee: better than ever.” Her MAGA credentials suggest she’s likely to select a successor with a similar profile, but that won’t be certain until her choice is formally announced. 
Throughout the campaign, Blackburn repeatedly declined to answer questions about who she might choose to replace her but said early on in the process that she intended to make the decision herself, rather than leaving it up to outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee. 
That hadn’t changed in the weeks since she was formally elected. She told Fox News on Nov. 15 that she hadn’t made up her mind and didn’t yet have a “short list” of potential replacements. 
“I’m focused on finishing the work in the Senate and transitioning to governor,” she said.
Blackburn’s coyness hasn’t stopped speculation about who her selection might be. In the days after Democrats’ decisive midterm performance earlier this month — which many top Republicans attributed to voters' dissatisfaction with the war in Iran — rumors began to spread that Blackburn might choose embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her seat. Those rumors were quickly refuted by sources close to Blackburn. 
The two names that have been most frequently suggested as Blackburn’s replacement are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett. 
Jacobs turned to politics after a long career in professional wrestling, where he performed as the horror-themed character Kane. He told Fox News in September that it would be a “huge honor” to be Blackburn’s chosen successor and he would “consider it very seriously” if asked. 
Burchett, who represents Tennessee’s deep red Second District in the House of Representatives, has said he “absolutely” wants to be considered for the position. He has also made clear that he intends to run for the Senate in 2028 against Blackburn’s pick if she chooses someone other than him. 
Blackburn is scheduled to be sworn in as governor on Jan. 16 and would likely appoint her replacement shortly after taking office. Whoever she chooses will hold her seat until the 2028 general election, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish out the remaining two years of her term. 
A battle brewing in Minnesota
When Minnesota’s Democratic Gov. Tim Walz abruptly dropped his bid for a third term in January, reports immediately began to circulate that Klobuchar was considering launching a bid to replace him. She made it official a few weeks later. A former presidential candidate with a strong record of success in statewide races, Klobuchar quickly became the frontrunner in the Minnesota governor's race. She easily defeated Republican Lisa Demuth on Election Day. She will be the first woman to serve as governor of her state as well when she’s sworn in on Jan. 4.
Like Blackburn, Klobuchar has said she intends to choose her own successor and has remained mum on who she may be considering. One name that can be crossed off the list is Walz, who said he would “rather eat glass” than take over her Senate seat. 
Under Minnesota law, Klobuchar’s successor would fill her seat on a temporary basis until November 2027, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish the remaining three years of her term. Because of that short time frame, Klobuchar has described the appointment as an “interim position.”
“It would be for about a year," she told a local news station last month.  
Nothing in Minnesota law bars appointees from running to keep their seat, but there is some recent history of governors filling vacancies with lawmakers who promise not to campaign for reelection. 
Replacements often end up holding on to their seats, however. Minnesota’s other senator, Tina Smith, was appointed to her seat in 2018 and has been reelected twice since then. Smith is retiring when her term ends in January.
Klobuchar could insist that her successor pledge to serve only as a temporary placeholder, but she hasn’t said whether she might disqualify potential candidates who decline to do so. 
Her selection, and the Senate race that will follow in November, could say a lot about the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. Midwest swing states were home to some of the most tightly contested midterm primary battles between progressive and moderate candidates anywhere in the country.
Minnesota’s Senate primary was won by the more left-leaning candidate, Peggy Flanagan. The same thing happened in nearby Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed eked out a primary win over moderate Haley Stevens. Both Flanagan and El-Sayed won their general election races earlier this month. 
This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/the-last-big-midterms-mystery-who-will-these-future-governors-choose-to-replace-them-in-the-senate-194352449.html

America is blessed and Tennessee: better than ever.” Her MAGA credentials suggest she’s likely to select a successor with a similar profile, but that won’t be certain until her choice is formally announced. 

Throughout the campaign, Blackburn repeatedly declined to answer questions about who she might choose to replace her but said early on in the process that she intended to make the decision herself, rather than leaving it up to outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee. 

That hadn’t changed in the weeks since she was formally elected. She told Fox News on Nov. 15 that she hadn’t made up her mind and didn’t yet have a “short list” of potential replacements. 

“I’m focused on finishing the work in the Senate and transitioning to governor,” she said.

Blackburn’s coyness hasn’t stopped speculation about who her selection might be. In the days after Democrats’ decisive midterm performance earlier this month — which many top Republicans attributed to voters' dissatisfaction with the war in Iran — rumors began to spread that Blackburn might choose embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her seat. Those rumors were quickly refuted by sources close to Blackburn. 

The two names that have been most frequently suggested as Blackburn’s replacement are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett. 

Jacobs turned to politics after a long career in professional wrestling, where he performed as the horror-themed character Kane. He told Fox News in September that it would be a “huge honor” to be Blackburn’s chosen successor and he would “consider it very seriously” if asked. 

Burchett, who represents Tennessee’s deep red Second District in the House of Representatives, has said he “absolutely” wants to be considered for the position. He has also made clear that he intends to run for the Senate in 2028 against Blackburn’s pick if she chooses someone other than him. 

Blackburn is scheduled to be sworn in as governor on Jan. 16 and would likely appoint her replacement shortly after taking office. Whoever she chooses will hold her seat until the 2028 general election, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish out the remaining two years of her term. 

A battle brewing in Minnesota

When Minnesota’s Democratic Gov. Tim Walz abruptly dropped his bid for a third term in January, reports immediately began to circulate that Klobuchar was considering launching a bid to replace him. She made it official a few weeks later. A former presidential candidate with a strong record of success in statewide races, Klobuchar quickly became the frontrunner in the Minnesota governor's race. She easily defeated Republican Lisa Demuth on Election Day. She will be the first woman to serve as governor of her state as well when she’s sworn in on Jan. 4.

Like Blackburn, Klobuchar has said she intends to choose her own successor and has remained mum on who she may be considering. One name that can be crossed off the list is Walz, who said he would “rather eat glass” than take over her Senate seat. 

Under Minnesota law, Klobuchar’s successor would fill her seat on a temporary basis until November 2027, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish the remaining three years of her term. Because of that short time frame, Klobuchar has described the appointment as an “interim position.”

“It would be for about a year," she told a local news station last month. 

Nothing in Minnesota law bars appointees from running to keep their seat, but there is some recent history of governors filling vacancies with lawmakers who promise not to campaign for reelection. 

Replacements often end up holding on to their seats, however. Minnesota’s other senator, Tina Smith, was appointed to her seat in 2018 and has been reelected twice since then. Smith is retiring when her term ends in January.

Klobuchar could insist that her successor pledge to serve only as a temporary placeholder, but she hasn’t said whether she might disqualify potential candidates who decline to do so. 

Her selection, and the Senate race that will follow in November, could say a lot about the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. Midwest swing states were home to some of the most tightly contested midterm primary battles between progressive and moderate candidates anywhere in the country.

Minnesota’s Senate primary was won by the more left-leaning candidate, Peggy Flanagan. The same thing happened in nearby Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed eked out a primary win over moderate Haley Stevens. Both Flanagan and El-Sayed won their general election races earlier this month.

title: NVDA Tanks 10% as SEC Reportedly Launches Nvidia Investigation
description: The stock price just dumped to $130.
fullContent:
Reports emerged minutes ago that the United States Securities and Exchange Commission has opened an investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices.

Citing people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal and Reuters reported that the agency will probe the company, but the actual focus of the investigation remains unclear at the moment.

Although details are scarce, the timing of the lawsuit is quite intriguing as it comes following the major scandal involving Nvidia’s co-founder and now former CEO, Jensen Huang.

The controversy began a few weeks ago after reports claimed that he had an extramarital relationship with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy. Although there’s no confirmation to this day whether she was indeed spying for Beijing, further reports indicated that he had a few more affairs with women working at Nvidia.

He broke his silence earlier this week, apologizing for his behavior and suggesting that he could return to the helm of the company he co-founded decades ago. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump urged Nvidia to reinstate him.

The lack of details from today’s SEC investigation reports couldn’t stop Nvidia’s stock price from dumping. NVDA has slumped by almost 11% during today’s trading session alone, dropping to $130 for the first time in a year and a half. The stock is down by almost 50% in less than two months.

title: Anthropic mathematician says AI helped him solve a 167-year-old math mystery
description:
Math's "white whale" may have just been cracked with the help of Anthropic's Claude.J Studios/Getty Images
A mathematician said on Friday that he cracked one of the biggest problems in mathematics.
Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said he used Claude to solve it.
Mathematicians told Business Insider the result hasn't been fully verified yet.

One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI.
Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude.
"I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet.
"If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale."
Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal."
"This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math."
Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes.
"So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said.
The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers.
The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem, meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category.
Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said.
Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time."
Alpöge, who joined Anthropic in 2024, said he actually solved the problem on Sunday, but decided to hold off on announcing it after speaking with CEO Dario Amodei and consulting with other mathematicians.
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, went public on the stock market on Thursday. As of Friday afternoon, the price of Anthropic shares has steadily declined.
Alpöge said he didn't want to release "slop" to the public, adding that he still doesn't fully understand the math involved.
Still, he said that as other mathematicians attempt to grapple with the results, Alpöge said he plans to be there every step of the way to help them.
"I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument," he said.
If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Dogecoin Plunges 15% in 1 Week as Whales Retreat: What Is Going On?
description:
Dogecoin (CRYPTO: DOGE) plunged 14.6% over the past week highlighting growing bearish pressure.
Large investors reduced exposure while retail traders remain heavily positioned for a rebound raising concerns about further downside.
CryptoQuant verified author Joao Wedson pointed to key derivatives indicators:
Long liquidations: $542.6 million (55%) versus $448.2 million in shorts (45%).
Whale vs. Retail Delta: -0.73, down 34% in seven days, signaling weakening whale participation relative to retail.
Open interest: $786 million, down 19% over the past week.
Long/short ratio: 2.90, indicating crowded bullish positioning.
Top traders’ ratio: 1.40, suggesting more balanced positioning among larger traders.
On-chain metrics also point to significant investor losses.
Critical Liquidity Zone
Wedson identified $0.053 as a critical downside liquidity zone, with major long liquidation clusters concentrated around, $0.0534 ($26.8 million), $0.0531 ($27.4 million) and $0.0528 ($23.4 million).
A decline toward these levels could trigger additional forced selling as leveraged long positions unwind.
Meanwhile, the nearest short liquidation clusters sit at $0.0649 and $0.0652, representing $7.5 million and $7 million, respectively.
Wedson warned that leverage continues to exit the market even as retail traders maintain bullish bets, leaving Dogecoin vulnerable to further liquidation-driven volatility.
Image: Shutterstock

title: SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme
The SEC obtained an asset freeze against Backward Hat Capital and its founders, alleging a $560 million Ponzi scheme sold as AI-driven FX trading funded through crypto. Prosecutors and the CFTC filed parallel cases.
This post SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme

The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.

The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022. A federal court granted a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze and expedited discovery to halt what the SEC called an ongoing scheme.

Federal prosecutors in New York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases. The SEC and CFTC suits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, and the CFTC said the court has appointed Kevin B. Duff as temporary receiver to take control of the companies and the individual defendants’ assets.

The pitch: crypto, AI and 6% a month

According to the SEC’s complaint, Williams and Johnson sold limited partnership interests in private funds through a network of promoters, including to Williams’s former investment advisory clients. They promised a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm that supposedly returned at least 6% every month by trading foreign exchange.

Investor money, the pitch went, would first be converted into a crypto asset and then used for that arbitrage. The complaint does not name bitcoin as the asset. It says about $109 million of the roughly $210 million raised from July 2022 to September 2025 was sent to the fund’s Coinbase account and converted.

Of that, more than $56 million went to personal crypto accounts held by Williams, Johnson and a relief defendant, according to the complaint. About $40 million ended up on three platforms where some of it was used to trade other crypto assets, but little to no money was used to trade FX. After October 2025, the scheme raised about $350 million, and none of it was sent to Coinbase.

Where the money went

The SEC said the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi payments to earlier investors and moved more than $220 million to themselves. The money paid for exotic cars, expensive homes, private air travel and other businesses they owned, and helped feed Johnson’s gambling. Promoters took more than $50 million.

Anderson is accused of producing fake financial reports, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report from a supposedly independent firm. The SEC said the documents falsely claimed the returns had been verified against bank and brokerage records. It said Anderson did no audit work, was not independent and had a financial stake in the scheme.

Prosecutors in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The FBI arrested Williams in Kokomo, Indiana, and Johnson in Gilbert, Arizona, on Wednesday. Prosecutors put the total raised at more than $600 million.

“As alleged, Phillip Patrick Williams and Devin Allen Johnson promised to use investor funds for profitable foreign exchange currency trading,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Williams and Johnson instead stole hundreds of millions of dollars from their investors for personal expenses and to pay off earlier investors in a Ponzi-like fashion.”

Regulators’ latest crypto fraud cases

The CFTC put the Ponzi at more than $550 million from at least 2,100 participants and said defendants kept soliciting money through at least October 2026. Its complaint seeks restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties, trading bans and a permanent injunction. The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties.

The case follows other recent enforcement actions tied to crypto-branded fraud. The SEC charged two companies in a $130 million crypto trading scheme last month, and New York sought a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of the NovaTech Ponzi scheme. In August, the CFTC charged Goliath Ventures with a $400 million bitcoin fraud.

Anne McKinley, acting associate director of the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office, said the promise of “a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money.”

This post SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.

title: Wealth Platforms Set Record for Bitcoin ETP Ownership Despite Market Weakness: Report
description: Galaxy's Q3 figures show advisors added 24,838 BTC-equivalent, accounting for roughly half of institutional managers' net purchases.
fullContent:
Financial advisors and wealth platforms increased their Bitcoin exchange-traded product (ETP) holdings to a record in the third quarter of 2026, despite recent price weakness.

This is according to a report shared by Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, which showed that this group now holds more than 40% of all reportable BTC ETP positions for clients.

Advisors Account for Over 40% of Reported Holdings

The report, published on November 19, puts advisors and wealth platforms holdings at 144,307 BTC-equivalent as of September 30. That represents 40.5% of all holdings reported by institutional managers that filed Form 13F with the SEC, and just over 11% of all Bitcoin held by the funds, with both figures being record highs.

BTC-equivalent refers to the amount of Bitcoin represented by an institution’s ETP shares, with Galaxy converting the reported share positions into corresponding amounts of the OG cryptocurrency, allowing holdings across different funds to be compared.

According to Thorn, holdings in the category have gone up for nine straight quarters and are now about 3.3 times above the level from March 2024. Advisors and wealth platforms also added 24,838 BTC-equivalent in Q3, which accounted for about half of the net additions reported by institutional filers.

The data also showed that most of that buying came from large financial institutions, with wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms contributing 22,728 BTC-equivalent. They were led by Wells Fargo with 14,636, followed by Bank of America and Morgan Stanley, with 7,201 and 2,875 BTC-equivalent, respectively.

Per the report, Wells Fargo is now the largest reported institutional holder, with 30,553 BTC-equivalent, which by the end of the quarter had been valued at approximately $2.55 billion. On the other hand, there were net reductions, including by Galaxy Digital, whose exposure went from the equivalent of 7,519 BTC to about 4,786.

Still, the number of managers holding spot BTC funds went up by 191 to hit 2,166, although these newcomers, per Thorn’s report, were relatively small holders, with less than 10,000 BTC-equivalent among them, compared to nearly 60,000 added by the 50 biggest holders.

BTC ETFs Have Hit a Rut

While the third-quarter data showed advisors and wealth platforms steadily accumulating Bitcoin exposure, more recent flows from one of the products tracking the cryptocurrency have been far weaker.

In Q3, spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net inflows running to over $6.3 billion, but Q4 hasn’t been as kind. Per data from SoSoValue, since October, the funds have bled more than $3.9 billion, with November alone seeing a run of 12 red days, interjected by modest inflows on November 4 and November 16.

Bitcoin itself hasn’t fared any better, and even plunged to a four-month low on Friday, on the back of Anthropic’s historic IPO. But ETF analyst and NovaDius Wealth President Nate Geraci noted that despite the current “rough” patch for the asset, investors putting money into its ecosystem were more focused on the long term.

“While everyone is melting down…Advisors & wealth platforms are now at record highs in bitcoin ETF ownership,” he wrote.

The post Wealth Platforms Set Record for Bitcoin ETP Ownership Despite Market Weakness: Report appeared first on CryptoPotato.

title: Solana Price Loses Its Summer Floor, June Low Back in View
description:
Key Takeaways Reclaim of the 0.786 level lasted one day Friday’s high stalled just under $74 Rally from June low […]
The post Solana Price Loses Its Summer Floor, June Low Back in View appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways
Reclaim of the 0.786 level lasted one day
Friday’s high stalled just under $74
Rally from June low is 87% erased
RSI near 23.5, oversold but not turning

The Level SOL Couldn’t Keep

When SOL traded near $79 a week ago, Coindoo’s November 13 analysis flagged the 0.786 Fibonacci retracement near $74 as the last level above $60. This week’s trading has revolved around that line. SOL broke below it within days, then closed back above it on November 17, near $75, for a single session. It slipped under the level again over the next two days, and Friday’s candle opened just below it, near $73. The high stopped roughly 35 cents short of the level before sellers pushed price to an intraday low near $68. As of 18:49 UTC, with about five hours left in the session, SOL traded near $69, down 6.14%.

The November 17 close also raises the bar for any recovery. One close above $75 has already happened and reversed within a day, so a reclaim that counts would need to hold for more than one session.

From Floor to Ceiling

The same level played the opposite role a few months ago.

July-August
The floor
The $73-$75 area was the base of a summer range SOL traded in for weeks. The 50-day average turned up from that zone in August, and the range became the launch point for September’s run to $125.
November
The ceiling
Since the mid-November break, the level has capped the bounce. It is now the first level any recovery has to retake.

87% of the Summer Rally Is Gone

June low to September high: what’s left
$60 · June low
87% given back
$125 · September high
Teal: the share of the rally SOL still holds at about $69.

Measured from the June low near $60 to the late-September peak at $125, SOL has given back about 87% of the rally and sits 45% below the high. Above price, the 0.618 retracement near $85 and the 200-day average at $89 sit close together, forming the next resistance band after the 0.786 level. Below, the full retracement near $60 is the only labeled level left. It marks the June low that the whole Fibonacci grid is drawn from.

What June Actually Looked Like

The space between Friday’s price and the June low has trading history on it. After the early-June plunge to near $60, SOL spent weeks moving between that low and the level it is now testing from below, with long wicks in both directions and a late-June pullback into the lower part of the range. None of that range carries a labeled level on this chart, but buyers and sellers have traded there before. Friday’s low near $68 is the first line to watch. Under it, the June range is the reference all the way down to the full retracement near $60.

Averages Above, Momentum Stretched

All three daily averages sit above price: the 100-day at $100, the 50-day at $97 and the 200-day at $89. The 50-day has just slipped under the 100-day as it turns sharply lower. It is still above the 200-day, so this isn’t the 50/200 “death cross,” but SOL trades about 22% below even the lowest of the three.

Momentum points the other way. The 14-day RSI reads 23.5, well inside oversold territory, and it is still under its own average near 24.1, so it hasn’t turned up. On this chart, the only comparable reading came in early June, at the low the Fibonacci grid starts from. Readings this low can persist through a strong selloff, and they can also produce sudden short-covering spikes, so the oversold reading cuts both ways.

Volume favors the sellers, with a caveat. It spiked on the mid-November breakdown, faded during the bounce, and picked up again on Friday: 2.91 million SOL with hours still left in the session, already above the bounce days. The candle isn’t finished, though, and it is still lighter than the breakdown days.

Outside the Chart

SOL’s slide ran through a busy stretch for the network. Solana completed its move to 200-millisecond slots on October 9, halving its original 400-millisecond target, according to the Solana Foundation’s upgrade page. SOL was trading above $100 at the time. Last weekend the network dropped its “mainnet beta” label and adopted Solana 1.0 as a shared version number, a change that CoinDesk noted doesn’t make transactions faster or affect holders. The Solana Foundation’s Breakpoint conference ran in London from November 15 to 17. None of it slowed the decline, and neither did long-range valuation work such as Bitwise’s $1,100 scenario, whose assumptions run out to 2031.

Fund flows line up more closely with the chart. US spot Solana ETFs took in $271.6 million in September, as SOL rallied to its high, then saw $143.7 million in net outflows in October as the breakdown began, according to CoinDesk. On November 18, Roundhill asked the SEC to withdraw its proposed Solana covered-call ETF, which had never sold a share. Friday’s drop also came alongside the wider market: Bitcoin briefly fell tog around $59,000.

Three Ways Out

Continuation
● Bounces stall in the $72-$74 zone, under the 0.786 level
● Friday’s low near $68 gives way
● The $61-$60 area comes into play, just above and then at the June low
Reversal setup
● Price sweeps below the June low near $60
● A fast daily close back above it, a swing failure
● RSI prints a higher low, a bullish divergence
● Only then does the path toward $74, then $85, reopen
Invalidation
● A daily close back above $75-$76
● It holds for more than one session, unlike November 17
● Friday’s breakdown becomes a bear trap, with the $85-$89 band as the next resistance

These are conditions, not a forecast. Until one of them triggers, SOL sits between a level it has failed to hold twice in a week and a low it hasn’t tested since June.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment or trading advice. The levels and scenarios above describe conditions on the chart, not predictions of future prices. Cryptocurrencies are highly volatile, and you should do your own research and consider your own risk tolerance before making any investment decision.

title: Morgan Stanley Ends Anthropic Stock Support After Just One Day
description:
Morgan Stanley used Anthropic's full greenshoe after one day, as ANT stock slid back toward its $83 IPO price.
The post Morgan Stanley Ends Anthropic Stock Support After Just One Day appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Anthropic’s stock is falling sharply, and Morgan Stanley, which was responsible for helping stabilize its price, has already ended a key support mechanism. It happened just one day after the biggest IPO in history.

Morgan Stanley had up to 30 days to use the mechanism. Instead, it closed the arrangement on Friday, as Anthropic shares approached their $83 IPO price.

The decision is good news for Anthropic’s fundraising, but raises fresh concerns for investors.

Why Did Morgan Stanley End Its Support So Early?

When Anthropic went public on Thursday, Morgan Stanley was responsible for helping stabilize its stock during early trading.

The bank had two options for covering 147 million additional shares sold to investors:

  • If Anthropic’s stock fell: Buy shares from the market, creating demand that could help slow the decline.
  • If the stock stayed above $83: Buy the additional shares directly from Anthropic at the original IPO price.

On Friday, Morgan Stanley chose the second option, purchasing all 147 million shares at $83 each.

This process is known as a greenshoe option. It closed the bank’s short position linked to those additional shares, removing a potential source of market buying support.

What Does This Mean for Anthropic Stock Investors?

For Anthropic, the decision brings another $12.2 billion in gross IPO proceeds, taking the offering’s total to approximately $93.5 billion.

For investors, the timing is concerning.

Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 on Thursday and briefly reached $115.10. They closed at $97.17 before falling as low as $83.93 in Friday’s premarket trading.

Anyone who bought near Thursday’s peak was already facing a roughly 27% loss.

Carsten Hesse, an analyst at Berenberg, told Reuters that investors were losing “an important potential source of buying support.”

The wider technology selloff is adding pressure.

The next major test is $83. If Anthropic falls below its IPO price, investors will face further losses without the potential buying support from Morgan Stanley’s now-closed arrangement.

That support was never guaranteed, and its removal does not mean another
