title: Solana’s Next Upgrade Could Break Existing Apps As Developers Face New Warning
description: Solana developers are facing a new compatibility warning as blockchain infrastructure team Anza prepares to introduce a major runtime improvement that could change how applications interact with network memory. The development comes just days after Solana officially exited beta, marking a new chapter for the blockchain’s infrastructure and development roadmap. On November 19, Anza announced […]
fullContent:
Solana developers are facing a new compatibility warning as blockchain infrastructure team Anza prepares to introduce a major runtime improvement that could change how applications interact with network memory.

The development comes just days after Solana officially exited beta, marking a new chapter for the blockchain’s infrastructure and development roadmap.

On November 19, Anza announced that mainnet feature activations were resuming following the Breakpoint conference, while warning that an upcoming change known as account data direct mapping could disrupt programs relying on certain memory-access behaviors.

Although the upgrade promises more efficient transaction execution, developers may need to review existing smart contracts before the changes are fully activated.

Solana Developers Receive Warning Over Direct Mapping

According to the Solana Foundation’s official technical documentation, direct mapping will change how validators handle account data during smart contract execution.

Currently, Solana’s runtime copies account information into a program’s virtual machine before execution and copies it back afterward.

Additional transfers can occur when programs interact through cross-program invocations, commonly known as CPIs.

The new system aims to eliminate these unnecessary copying operations by allowing programs to access account data directly.

Under the existing approach, certain instructions can involve up to four data-copy operations. Direct mapping is designed to reduce that number to zero.

However, achieving this efficiency requires stricter rules governing memory access.

Programs that previously relied on unsupported shortcuts may encounter errors once the relevant restrictions are activated.

Which Solana Applications Could Be Affected?

The warning does not mean that every Solana application is at risk.

According to the Solana Foundation, most programs should continue functioning normally. However, developers using particular memory-management techniques may need to update their code.

Potential problems include reading beyond an account’s allocated memory, modifying read-only data, accessing multiple memory regions in a single operation, or relying on outdated account-resizing methods.

Applications built using older versions of Anchor may also encounter compatibility issues involving account ownership during cross-program interactions.

The Foundation recommends that affected developers upgrade to Anchor version 1.2.2 and rebuild their programs.

Another concern involves changes to stack memory. Unlike ordinary instruction failures, certain stack-related problems could alter application behavior without immediately generating an error.

This makes comprehensive testing particularly important.

Anza has encouraged developers to test their applications using Solana’s development networks before the changes reach mainnet.

Why Solana Is Making These Changes

The proposed upgrade reflects Solana’s continuing effort to improve execution efficiency while supporting increasingly complex decentralized applications.

By removing repeated account-data copying, validators could reduce unnecessary processing work during certain transactions.

The benefits may be particularly relevant for applications handling large accounts or executing multiple cross-program interactions.

The development follows Solana’s recent Alpenglow upgrade, which introduced a redesigned consensus system targeting transaction finality of approximately 150 milliseconds.

However, the two upgrades address different aspects of blockchain performance.

Alpenglow focuses on how quickly validators finalize transactions, while direct mapping targets the efficiency of executing programs.

Together, these developments illustrate how Solana is improving different components of its infrastructure.

When Will Direct Mapping Reach Mainnet?

Although Anza has indicated that direct mapping is approaching mainnet activation, the Solana Foundation has not confirmed an activation date.

The rollout involves two separate feature gates.

The first, virtual_address_space_adjustments, introduces stricter memory-access rules. The second, account_data_direct_mapping, eliminates the copying operations.

Both have already undergone activation on Solana’s development and testing networks.

However, published sources have shown differences in the reported mainnet status of the first gate, making further confirmation important.

The actual direct-mapping feature remains pending.

What This Means For SOL And The Wider Ecosystem

The upgrade arrives as Solana continues expanding its infrastructure to accommodate more demanding blockchain applications.

For developers, the immediate priority is ensuring that existing programs comply with the new memory restrictions.

For investors, the development highlights both the opportunities and challenges associated with upgrading a high-performance blockchain.

More efficient execution could improve Solana’s long-term capacity to support decentralized finance, payments, and other applications.

However, successful implementation will depend on compatibility testing and a carefully managed activation process.

The announcement alone does not establish a direct impact on SOL’s market price.

As the network continues evolving, developers and investors will be watching how Anza manages the transition.

Ultimately, Solana’s next performance improvement could make its infrastructure more efficient, but ensuring existing applications remain reliable will be just as important as the speed gains themselves.

title: Solana’s Next Upgrade Could Break Existing Apps As Developers Face New Warning
description: Solana developers are facing a new compatibility warning as blockchain infrastructure team Anza prepares to introduce a major runtime improvement that could change how applications interact with network memory. The development comes just days after Solana officially exited beta, marking a new chapter for the blockchain’s infrastructure and development roadmap. On November 19, Anza announced […]
fullContent:
Solana developers are facing a new compatibility warning as blockchain infrastructure team Anza prepares to introduce a major runtime improvement that could change how applications interact with network memory.

The development comes just days after Solana officially exited beta, marking a new chapter for the blockchain’s infrastructure and development roadmap.

On November 19, Anza announced that mainnet feature activations were resuming following the Breakpoint conference, while warning that an upcoming change known as account data direct mapping could disrupt programs relying on certain memory-access behaviors.

Although the upgrade promises more efficient transaction execution, developers may need to review existing smart contracts before the changes are fully activated.

Solana Developers Receive Warning Over Direct Mapping

According to the Solana Foundation’s official technical documentation, direct mapping will change how validators handle account data during smart contract execution.

Currently, Solana’s runtime copies account information into a program’s virtual machine before execution and copies it back afterward.

Additional transfers can occur when programs interact through cross-program invocations, commonly known as CPIs.

The new system aims to eliminate these unnecessary copying operations by allowing programs to access account data directly.

Under the existing approach, certain instructions can involve up to four data-copy operations. Direct mapping is designed to reduce that number to zero.

However, achieving this efficiency requires stricter rules governing memory access.

Programs that previously relied on unsupported shortcuts may encounter errors once the relevant restrictions are activated.

Which Solana Applications Could Be Affected?

The warning does not mean that every Solana application is at risk.

According to the Solana Foundation, most programs should continue functioning normally. However, developers using particular memory-management techniques may need to update their code.

Potential problems include reading beyond an account’s allocated memory, modifying read-only data, accessing multiple memory regions in a single operation, or relying on outdated account-resizing methods.

Applications built using older versions of Anchor may also encounter compatibility issues involving account ownership during cross-program interactions.

The Foundation recommends that affected developers upgrade to Anchor version 1.2.2 and rebuild their programs.

Another concern involves changes to stack memory. Unlike ordinary instruction failures, certain stack-related problems could alter application behavior without immediately generating an error.

This makes comprehensive testing particularly important.

Anza has encouraged developers to test their applications using Solana’s development networks before the changes reach mainnet.

Why Solana Is Making These Changes

The proposed upgrade reflects Solana’s continuing effort to improve execution efficiency while supporting increasingly complex decentralized applications.

By removing repeated account-data copying, validators could reduce unnecessary processing work during certain transactions.

The benefits may be particularly relevant for applications handling large accounts or executing multiple cross-program interactions.

The development follows Solana’s recent Alpenglow upgrade, which introduced a redesigned consensus system targeting transaction finality of approximately 150 milliseconds.

However, the two upgrades address different aspects of blockchain performance.

Alpenglow focuses on how quickly validators finalize transactions, while direct mapping targets the efficiency of executing programs.

Together, these developments illustrate how Solana is improving different components of its infrastructure.

When Will Direct Mapping Reach Mainnet?

Although Anza has indicated that direct mapping is approaching mainnet activation, the Solana Foundation has not confirmed an activation date.

The rollout involves two separate feature gates.

The first, virtual_address_space_adjustments, introduces stricter memory-access rules. The second, account_data_direct_mapping, eliminates the copying operations.

Both have already undergone activation on Solana’s development and testing networks.

However, published sources have shown differences in the reported mainnet status of the first gate, making further confirmation important.

The actual direct-mapping feature remains pending.

What This Means For SOL And The Wider Ecosystem

The upgrade arrives as Solana continues expanding its infrastructure to accommodate more demanding blockchain applications.

For developers, the immediate priority is ensuring that existing programs comply with the new memory restrictions.

For investors, the development highlights both the opportunities and challenges associated with upgrading a high-performance blockchain.

More efficient execution could improve Solana’s long-term capacity to support decentralized finance, payments, and other applications.

However, successful implementation will depend on compatibility testing and a carefully managed activation process.

The announcement alone does not establish a direct impact on SOL’s market price.

As the network continues evolving, developers and investors will be watching how Anza manages the transition.

Ultimately, Solana’s next performance improvement could make its infrastructure more efficient, but ensuring existing applications remain reliable will be just as important as the speed gains themselves.

title: Hyperliquid Anthropic Volume Explodes Past $1.7B as Hong Kong Issues Warning
description:
Hyperliquid Anthropic trading volume hits $1.7B, overtaking ETH as Hong Kong's SFC flags the exchange over suspected unlicensed operations.
The post Hyperliquid Anthropic Volume Explodes Past $1.7B as Hong Kong Issues Warning appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Hyperliquid Anthropic trading market has surged to $1.7 billion in daily volume, pushing the contract ahead of Ethereum on the platform. The surge comes just as Hong Kong’s financial regulator adds Hyperliquid to its suspicious virtual asset trading platform list.

The ANT perpetual contract recorded $1.727 billion in trading volume over 24 hours on November 20. This has placed it second among Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets, behind Bitcoin but ahead of Ethereum.

Open interest also climbed to $259 million as traders built substantial positions rather than simply passing through short-term trades. The figures put Anthropic market in Hyperliquid among the exchange’s most active markets, despite tracking a company outside the traditional crypto sector.

Hyperliquid Anthropic Market Overtakes Ethereum

Just a day earlier, Anthropic ranked 17th among Hyperliquid perpetual contracts by trading volume. It then climbed to second place as activity accelerated around Anthropic’s public market debut. Its $1.727 billion turnover was 1.88 times Ethereum’s trading volume during the same period. Only Bitcoin attracted more activity, recording $5.139 billion.

The shift also displays how much Hyperliquid’s trading activity now extends beyond crypto-native assets. Six of the exchange’s top ten perpetual markets by volume were linked to traditional financial assets.

These included Anthropic, the XYZ100 technology index, the S&P 500, Nvidia, a leveraged semiconductor ETF, and South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix. Together, those six contracts generated $4.269 billion in volume, accounting for 38.1% of the top ten’s combined turnover.

ANT’s market has also attracted significant leverage. The contract allows traders to speculate on Anthropic’s share price using crypto collateral, without purchasing or owning the underlying shares.

Unlike conventional stock markets, the perpetual contract continues trading around the clock. This gives traders a venue to react to developments outside Nasdaq’s regular trading hours. This flexibility has helped attract activity as traders position themselves around major developments affecting the artificial intelligence sector.

Bitcoin Hyper Eyes Bigger Bitcoin DeFi Opportunity Ahead of Launch

Hyperliquid has demonstrated how much demand exists for trading assets beyond traditional crypto. Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a different opportunity: bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a much larger decentralized finance ecosystem.

The project is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. Its goal is to let BTC holders move beyond simply holding their coins, opening access to faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications.

That ambition is attracting considerable presale interest. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.29 million, with its token currently priced at just $0.01368760. More than 114,000 participants have joined the presale, giving the project considerable early fundraising momentum.

Staking is another major attraction, with the project offering rewards of up to 35% APY. That gives early participants an additional incentive to accumulate HYPER before its exchange debut, although actual rewards depend on the staking terms and participation.

Time is also becoming a factor. Bitcoin Hyper has scheduled its presale conclusion for November 26, putting its anticipated launch just days away. With the token still available below two cents, the approaching deadline could intensify demand among investors looking to secure an early position.

Gain Access to New Bitcoin Layer 2 Early Before the Presale Window Ends In 2 Weeks

Hong Kong Adds Hyperliquid to Suspicious Platform List

The trading surge comes against a growing regulatory problem for Hyperliquid. Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission added Hyperliquid and Hyperliquid Hong Kong to its suspicious virtual asset trading platforms list. The regulator specifically identified the platform’s trading interface at app.hyperliquid.xyz, stating that the entity was not licensed by the SFC.

The watchdog suspects the platform of operating, holding itself out as operating, or actively marketing an unlicensed virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public.

The warning puts Hyperliquid under scrutiny in one of Asia’s most important financial centers. Hong Kong has spent recent years developing a licensing framework for crypto exchanges, requiring platforms serving local investors to obtain regulatory authorization.

The SFC also warned that investors using unlicensed platforms could lose their entire investment if an operator collapses, suffers a hack, or misappropriates customer assets.

fullContent:
The bleeding this November appears relentless, producing yet another consecutive red day for crypto. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost a net $582 million on Thursday, November 19, their third straight day of outflows, and BTC USD slipped under $62,000.

Nov 19 Update:#Bitcoin ETFs:
1D NetFlow: -4,658 $BTC(-$296.7M)
7D NetFlow: -15,314 $BTC(-$975.49M)#Ethereum ETFs:
1D NetFlow: -9,904 $ETH(-$17.85M)
7D NetFlow: -65,373 $ETH(-$117.82M) pic.twitter.com/rbMJlxphrQ

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) November 19, 2026

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541 million of that, its largest single-day outflow since it launched in January 2024. Only Morgan Stanley’s new fund, MSBT, took in money, about $49.6 million.

The selling has been steady all month. The funds have lost money on 12 of 14 trading days in November, a net $3.47 billion. At each day’s closing price, that is about 49,400 BTC. Over the same stretch, Bitcoin fell 20%, from $77,582 at the end of October to $61,987 on Thursday.

So when do the ETF sellers run out, and where does BTC USD find a floor?

BTC USD ETF Flows: $3.47 Billion Out in November

Thursday’s outflow was the biggest single day of the month. Here’s how the funds split it up:

  • BlackRock (IBIT): -$541.1 million, about 93% of the day’s total. IBIT has lost about $2.9 billion in November, more than any other fund.
  • Fidelity (FBTC): -$45.9 million.
  • ARK 21Shares (ARKB): -$31.3 million.
  • Grayscale (GBTC): -$13.9 million.
  • Morgan Stanley (MSBT): +$49.6 million, the only fund with inflows, bringing its total since launch to $888 million.

Even after this month, the US funds are far from empty. They hold about $76.6 billion, around 6.1% of Bitcoin’s market value, and investors have still put in a net $53.5 billion since January 2024. The funds update their holdings daily, and IBIT’s own figures are on BlackRock’s iShares page.

Institutions added 49,229 BTC to US spot ETFs in Q3, their biggest quarterly buy since Q2 2025. Total holdings are a record 356,491 BTC (per Galaxy’s Alex Thorn).

Price is lower now, but the stack keeps growing. pic.twitter.com/7BKdPWXxlc

— 𝕮𝖗𝖞𝖕𝖙𝖔 𝖂𝖆𝖗𝖗𝖎𝖔𝖗 (@ScottLEOWarrior) November 20, 2026

DISCOVER: Top 20 Crypto to Buy in 2026

Big Outflow Days Hit Bitcoin Hardest: Fed Fears and Falling Tech Stocks Drive the Selling

We lined up the daily ETF flow tables from November 2 to 19 with Binance’s daily BTC candles. We split the 14 trading days in two: seven days with outflows of $250 million or more, and seven days with smaller outflows or inflows.

  • The big days: on the seven heaviest outflow days, BTC fell 2.2% on average.
  • The rest: on the other seven days, BTC moved just -0.2% on average.
  • The exceptions: the link isn’t perfect. On November 11, $300 million left the funds and BTC still rose 0.3%. On November 13, a smaller $186 million outflow came with a 4.4% drop.

ETF flows are counted on the US trading day, while our BTC moves use the UTC calendar day, so the two don’t line up exactly. The direction still holds: when ETF holders sell hard, BTC USD drops, because other buyers haven’t been strong enough to absorb it.

DISCOVER: Bitcoin Below Its 200-Week Average for the First Time Since 2022: Is a Drop to $50K Coming or a Historic Buying Opportunity?

The ETF selling isn’t happening in a vacuum. On Thursday, the S&P 500 fell 2% for its sixth straight loss on the day Anthropic listed on Nasdaq. Bitcoin has been moving closely with tech stocks: its 40-day correlation with the Nasdaq 100 has climbed to 0.69, Bloomberg reported. A reading of 1 would mean they move in lockstep.

Paul Howard, a senior director at trading firm Wincent, pointed to the same mix.

ETF outflows and the Fed’s hawkish posture are weighing on risk assets

he told Bloomberg. Traders expect the Federal Reserve to keep rates high, which tends to hurt Bitcoin and tech stocks alike.

Not everyone thinks the selling is done. “I don’t think that flushing out is over yet,” Raj Kamal, chief executive of crypto payments firm TransFi, told AMBCrypto.

DISCOVER: Best New Cryptocurrencies to Invest in 2026

BTC USD Price Analysis: $62,300 Turns Into Resistance

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $61,939. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $74,658, and its 200-day EMA at $75,470.

  • Resistance: $62,300, the floor Bitcoin held in June, July, August and twice this month, now acting as a ceiling. Above that, $65,500.
  • Support: $58,500, where Bitcoin turned in June and again on July 1.
Path What has to happen Next stop
Push higher A daily close back above $62,300, with ETF flows turning positive $65,500, the June-August ceiling
Stall Price stays between $58,500 and $62,300 A range below the old floor
Slip A daily close below $58,500 $57,800, the July 1 low, then lower

For BTC USD, the daily ETF flow is the number to watch. A few days of inflows like Monday’s would ease the pressure on $58,500. Another $500 million day like Thursday’s would make that support much harder to hold.

title: Is Bitcoin Dead? Jack Mallers Points to Its History
description:
Key Takeaways Bitcoin trades below its 50, 100, 200-day averages Price sits just above this year’s lows Mallers’ own sentiment […]
The post Is Bitcoin Dead? Jack Mallers Points to Its History appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Bitcoin trades below its 50, 100, 200-day averages
  • Price sits just above this year’s lows
  • Mallers’ own sentiment data carries a warning
  • Fed balance sheet runoff ended in December 2025

In the November 17 edition of The Jack Mallers Show, the Strike CEO argued that Bitcoin’s slide looks like earlier bear markets that investors wrongly took for the end. Strike sells Bitcoin services, so Mallers benefits when demand for the asset grows.

Mallers’ Case: Bitcoin Has Been Here Before

Mallers has held Bitcoin for almost 14 years, and his argument rests on that memory. Every bear market he has lived through came with the same verdict that Bitcoin was finished. Walking through the major crashes, from Mt. Gox to FTX, he notes that each of them cut deeper than the current decline.

Bear market Peak-to-low loss
2011 93%
2013 to 2015 84% to 85%
2017 to 2018 84%
2021 to 2022 77%
2025 to 2026, still open 54% at the July low, about 51% on November 20

Rounded figures from Glassnode’s cycle research and exchange price histories. Intraday extremes and daily closes produce slightly different percentages.

Mallers reads the current cycle as a sign of strength rather than fatigue. Bitcoin set its October 2025 record more than 80% above its 2021 peak while the Federal Reserve was still running down its balance sheet, so the rally came without the flood of new money that powered 2021.

The comparison only covers the damage done so far. The earlier rows describe finished cycles measured to their final lows, while this one is 410 days old and has no confirmed low. Maller points out that the previous gaps between record highs ran about three years, three years and 2.3 years, which makes a year spent below the peak ordinary rather than alarming.

Where the Chart Is Testing That Claim

At 09:19 UTC on November 20, Bitcoin traded at $61,663 on Binance, about 51% below its record above $126,000. On the daily chart the price sits under all three of its main moving averages. It is roughly 15% beneath the 200-day average at $72,603, and further still below the 50-day at $77,772 and the 100-day at $77,748. Those two shorter lines are now only $24 apart and turning lower together.

Momentum is stretched. The 14-day RSI has dropped to around 20, a reading comparable to the ones Bitcoin printed near its February and June lows. Both times, the selling stalled and price rebounded within weeks.

That zone is the real test of Mallers’ argument. February’s sell-off stopped close to $60,000, and the July 1 low came in near $57,700. Price is now less than $2,000 above the top of that range, which would make this the third visit of the year. Daily closes holding inside it would give his history lesson its first chart support. A close below $57,700 would mark a new low for the cycle and push the drawdown past 54%.

Mallers also cites the slower 200-week moving average, which he places around $68,000, about 9% above today’s price. By his count, Bitcoin has spent less than a tenth of its life below that line. Coindoo’s November monthly-chart analysis flagged the low-$60,000 region as a structural level earlier this month.

The “Five Flat Years” Complaint Depends on the Start Date

The line Mallers hears most often is that Bitcoin has gone nowhere in five years. He answers it by pointing out that the same complaint was true in late 2022, shortly before the price rose roughly eightfold. Two windows of the same length, one year apart, show how much the starting point decides the answer.

Bought on Dec 31 Value five years later Return
2017 at $14,156 $16,548 About 17%
2018 at $3,743 $42,265 About 1,029%

Coindoo calculations from year-end daily closes. Nominal returns before fees, taxes or inflation.

A buyer at the end of 2017 waited five years to make 17%. A buyer twelve months later made more than ten times their money over the same span. A five-year figure says more about when someone bought than about the asset itself.

The Warning Inside Mallers’ Own Evidence

The strongest counterpoint in the episode came from a clip Mallers played himself, in the santiment segment. In it, sentiment researcher Michael Sullivan shows newer Bitcoin investors growing more optimistic while veterans of a decade or more turn less hopeful. Sullivan says gaps this wide have historically appeared around market tops, not bottoms, and his October 29 research note tracks the same drop in veteran optimism.

Mallers adds that, by Sullivan’s measures, sentiment is now worse than when Bitcoin traded near $58,000 and worse than during the March 2020 crash. Widespread fear is what most investors look for at a bottom. A split in which newcomers stay hopeful while the most experienced holders lose faith is a different picture. It suggests one group has not yet given up, and the group losing conviction is the one holding the oldest coins. Sullivan’s categories track online sentiment, not wallets, so they show mood rather than actual selling.

The gloom reaches well beyond crypto. The University of Michigan’s preliminary November survey put consumer sentiment at 51.0, up slightly from October’s 48.0, which Mallers notes was below the 2022 low. His slide adds a separate Michigan series, the share of consumers who say higher prices left them worse off than a year earlier. He puts it at 57%, and the Bloomberg chart he shows places it at its highest level since the late 1970s.

Who Is Selling Into the Drop

New bitcoins arrive only on a fixed schedule through mining, as Bitcoin.org explains, so a rise in demand has to be met by existing holders willing to sell. In Mallers’ view, tops form when prices climb high enough to pull long-held coins out of cold storage, and bottoms form once that selling dries up.

Glassnode’s November 16 Market Pulse shows that handover still in progress. The ratio of short-term to long-term holder supply barely moved, at 15.1% against 15.0% a week earlier, while recent buyers were sitting on losses on average and spot ETFs kept recording outflows. None of those readings yet shows sellers running out.

Some of the buying that does appear is recycled. Coindoo’s look at dip buying alongside dollars leaving crypto found investors rotating out of other tokens into Bitcoin rather than bringing in fresh money.

Mallers also cited new filings showing that Wells Fargo and Paul Tudor Jones had doubled their stakes in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust. The SEC filings list about 49.58 million shares for Wells Fargo and 1.36 million for Tudor Investment, plus separate options positions. Those holdings are as of September 30, seven weeks before November’s slide.

Liquidity Is Looser on Paper Than Mallers Implies

Mallers’ larger explanation for the decline is tight dollar liquidity. Opening the episode at 2:48, he points to the MOVE index of bond volatility, which he says has moved from its usual 60 to 80 range to above 100. Volatile Treasuries make weaker collateral, and that tightens financing across markets. He puts the level where authorities have historically stepped in at around 130. On top of that, heavy refinancing of short-term government debt and the AI spending boom are competing for the same capital.

The Federal Reserve is no longer adding to that squeeze. It ended its securities runoff on December 1, 2025, and its November 19 balance-sheet release shows average securities holdings near $6.47 trillion, about $208 billion higher than a year earlier. With the Fed’s portfolio growing again, the pressure Mallers describes has to come from the bond market and Treasury financing instead.

Old Fears, New Labels

Mallers argues that each bear market revives the same doubts under new names. Repeating a fear does not dismiss it, though, and each one is settled by different evidence.

Paper Bitcoin distorts the price

First raised when CME futures launched in 2017, now aimed at ETFs. Settled by spot versus derivatives volumes and ETF creation data.

Something better replaces it

Once Ethereum and altcoins, now AI. Settled by capital flows and Bitcoin’s performance against rivals, which Mallers says still favours it.

Governments ban it

China banned trading and mining in 2021. The US approved spot ETFs in 2024. Settled by policy, not price.

Quantum computing breaks it

A technical risk with no precedent in past cycles. Settled by progress on quantum-resistant signatures, which no price recovery can show.

What Would Settle the Test

Mallers is not asking anyone to trust a chart pattern. His claim is that sellers eventually run out, as they have in every previous cycle. These are the readings that would show whether that is happening this time.

  • Daily closes holding between roughly $57,700 and $60,000, or breaking below them
  • A move back above the 200-day average, the nearest of the three daily averages
  • The short-to-long-term holder ratio stalling and recent-buyer losses narrowing
  • ETF flows turning positive with new money rather than rotation from other tokens

Mallers ended the episode by telling listeners who want out to sell, because he is buying. The daily closes near $60,000 will show how many of the coins he is waiting for are still for sale.

The post Bitcoin Price Has Never Had Two Red Years in a Row: 4-Year Cycle Broken? appeared first on 99Bitcoins.
fullContent:
Bitcoin price is heading toward an unprecedented moment in its trading history. Bitcoin has fallen 30% in 2026, following a losing year in 2025. If sellers maintain control through December, BTC will record its first two consecutive negative calendar years.

The pattern has survived every major crypto winter. Bitcoin finished 2014 lower before recovering in 2015. It rebounded in 2019 after the brutal 2018 collapse, then climbed again in 2023 following the FTX-driven crash. This time, however, the recovery has failed to arrive on schedule.

BTC is hovering at the $61,900 level, extending a sharp November selloff. The token has fallen 51% from its October 2025 record near $126,200.

So, is the 4-year cycle broken for the first time?

Market Cap

Bitcoin Price History: Recovery Pattern Under Threat

Bitcoin’s annual performance has been anything but consistent, but its losing years have shared one important characteristic: none has been followed by another annual loss.

In 2014, Bitcoin price dropped 56% before gaining 35% in 2015. The 2018 bear market wiped out 73% of its value, but BTC recovered around 92% the following year.

The same pattern appeared after the 2022 collapse. Bitcoin lost 64% that year, then surged more than 155% in 2023 as investors returned and expectations surrounding spot Bitcoin ETFs grew.

BTC USD, TradingView

Bitcoin also finished 2025 6.3% lower, despite reaching a new all-time high above $126,000 in October. Its current decline puts 2026 on course to extend that losing streak. Bitcoin has also already experienced another post-halving year without delivering the familiar annual rally. The market is approaching December with big losses and weakening momentum.

DISCOVER: 15+ Best Crypto IPO to Watch in 2026

Technical Analysis Points to Further Pressure

The daily chart offers little evidence that sellers have exhausted themselves. Bitcoin trades below its 50-day moving average at $78,200 and its 200-day average around $72,700.

Its 14-day relative strength index has fallen close to 20, firmly inside oversold territory. That reading signals intense selling pressure, and it does not show an immediate reversal.

BTC USD, TradingView

The daily structure also shows lower highs and lower lows. BTC’s decline has pushed it toward the $60,000 region as buyers fail to defend the nearby support.

The first important support zone sits around $60,850, followed by $59,700. A sustained break below those levels could expose Bitcoin to another wave of selling.

On the upside, $64,850 represents an initial resistance level. Reclaiming that area would offer an early indication that buyers are returning, while a move toward $67,200 would provide stronger evidence of recovery.

For now, the gap between Bitcoin market price and its major moving averages highlights how much ground bulls must recover.

DISCOVER: 15+ Upcoming Coinbase Listings to Watch in 2026

Bitcoin’s Four-Year Cycle Finally Breaking?

This Bitcoin price decline challenges the traditional halving cycle. Previous halvings preceded major bull markets, with rallies generally peaking the following year before deep corrections.

The 2024 halving followed that pattern, but the subsequent price action has been far less convincing. Institutional participation, spot ETF demand, and changing macroeconomic conditions have altered the market structure.

The arrival of regulated investment products has brought new sources of demand, but it has not eliminated Bitcoin’s exposure to financial markets. Risk aversion can still trigger rapid withdrawals and aggressive selling.

The next few weeks could carry unusual historical significance. A recovery before year-end would preserve Bitcoin’s record of avoiding consecutive annual losses. Now it looks like another close in negative territory will end that streak for the first time.

Spot candles show XMR1 trading near $494 before the dump. Within about 35 minutes the book printed near $1. That is a drop of roughly 99 percent. Afterwards, Wagyu's PerpetualCow said the dump traced to a compromised host, not a Hyperliquid market bug.

Dump Wallet Sells Into the Book

On Hyperliquid, deployer address 0x2077…e06a sent three spot transfers of XMR1 to 0x1464…20Bf. The first transfer moved 100,000 XMR1 at about 04:47 UTC on 20 November 2026. Two more sends followed, for 100,000 and then 5,000,000 XMR1. The three transfers total 5.2 million tokens. Hypurrscan shows the receiving wallet selling into the spot book soon after. Afterwards, that address routed about $13.28 million USDC through Hyperliquid spot settlement. Lookonchain reported the same flow and said the seller spent about $13.22 million USDC to buy roughly 7,467 ETH.

On the other hand, Scam Sniffer had labeled the activity a suspected theft of the deployer wallet before Wagyu spoke. Crypto Banter shared PerpetualCow's claim that the entire 1984.hosting infrastructure was compromised today. He said customer data and internal server files were exposed. Moreover, he said the XMR1 deployer key still sat on an old server he had already deleted. At the moment, he says everyone who lost money will be refunded personally and that Wagyu will relaunch later. Nowadays that pattern sits at the center of many crypto hacks that never touch a smart-contract bug.

What Traders Saw on Hyperliquid

The crash was a liquidity event first. The dump wallet emptied size into a thin spot book. Afterwards, mid prices collapsed from the mid-$490s toward about $1. On the other hand, Hyperliquid still showed XMR1 listed with a prior-day mark near $502 after the sell wave. At the moment, residual balance on 0x1464…20Bf still holds millions of XMR1. Lookonchain also asked whether XMR1 itself had been hacked. The public evidence answers a narrower question. Someone with deployer access moved 5.2 million tokens. Someone then sold hard and bought ETH with the USDC proceeds.

What the XMR1 Hyperliquid Hack Leaves Open

Wrapped Monero on a perpetual venue trades on trust in the deployer wallet and the host that stores it. Afterwards, holders who marked XMR1 near $500 learned how fast that trust can fail. On the other hand, PerpetualCow now ties the key loss to the 1984.hosting breach and pledges personal refunds. At the moment, readers who track crypto hacks will watch three points next: whether refunds clear, whether Wagyu relaunches, and where the ETH goes. Until those answers arrive, Friday's tape stands as a 99 percent wipe after a 5.2 million token deployer dump on Hyperliquid.

title: Trump Memecoin Dinner? Investors Wait for a Miracle

Trump memecoin dinner back on the table as holders face 99% losses, MELANIA slides and WLFI struggles to regain investor confidence.
The post Trump Memecoin Dinner? Investors Wait for a Miracle appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Donald Trump is preparing another exclusive dinner for his biggest memecoin supporters, but the invitation is becoming cheaper as his token continues to collapse. The TRUMP token is down almost 99% from its peak, and this time, the presidential dinner contest closed with just 130 participating wallets holding $8.6 million, despite organizers offering 185 places.

The dinner will welcome the largest holders at Trump’s Virginia golf club on November 22. The top 29 receive an additional VIP reception, while other token holders are left watching from outside.

Just last year, wealthy buyers competed for access to Trump with millions of dollars in token purchases. This time, more than 5,000 eligible holders reportedly declined to register, while one successful entrant qualified with just $518 in purchases.

The upcoming celebration offers little reason to celebrate, as holders watched millions disappear from their holdings during the competition.

Trump Memecoin VIP Dinner Comes, Investors Run Out of Reasons to Celebrate

The shrinking competition exposes a problem that another presidential appearance cannot easily fix. TRUMP first memecoin dinner generated considerable excitement around the token, attracting buyers who wanted proximity to Trump and exposure to his political brand. That enthusiasm has since faded alongside the price.

Trump’s family has reportedly earned at least $635 million from the memecoin through April, according to financial disclosures and reported estimates. Meanwhile, outside investors have suffered substantial losses across several Trump-linked crypto ventures.

So, what happens to everyone who bought the token but never gets an invitation?

There is no comparable VIP experience for ordinary investors who purchased during the rally and are now sitting on losses. They cannot simply exchange their depreciated holdings for access to the president.

MELANIA and WLFI Add to Trump’s Growing Crypto Problem

The frustration extends beyond TRUMP. MELANIA memecoin has also suffered a dramatic collapse from its launch-era highs, weakening confidence in the wider family-branded token ecosystem. Investors who bought into the political momentum now face a difficult question about what sustains demand once the initial excitement disappears.

World Liberty Financial is another broken painting. Its WLFI governance token has fallen towards $0.045, close to its all-time low of $0.0437. A substantial retreat from its September 2025 peak near $0.33.

Its USD1 stablecoin has also seen its market cap retreat from $4.4 billion in early October to around $2.9 billion today.

These are different products with different purposes, but their declining market valuations put pressure on the Trump-linked crypto narrative.

From bad comes to worse. Justin Sun, Tron founder, was among the most prominent early supporters of World Liberty Financial and attended Trump’s inaugural memecoin dinner. His WLFI holdings were frozen by the project, prompting him to file a lawsuit against the company just a few months ago.

The concern is no longer simply if all of Trump’s linked tokens can recover.

Iran War Adds Another Headache for Trump’s Crypto Supporters

The market environment is hardly helping speculative assets. Iran war continues to disrupt commercial shipping and keep geopolitical risk in financial markets. Renewed attacks around Riyadh and reported tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil prices higher on Friday.

Brent crude hovers at $92, while US West Texas Intermediate reached $83. Both benchmarks were nevertheless heading for another weekly decline as expectations of a global supply surplus offset renewed geopolitical concerns.

For us, the problem extends beyond oil prices. Energy disruptions can feed inflation concerns, complicate interest-rate expectations and undermine appetite for riskier investments.

Memecoins have little protection when speculative demand disappears. The political branding behind the TRUMP memecoin cannot guarantee buyers will return after the dinner, especially when holders are dealing with substantial losses.

Trump can still host another dinner and welcome his biggest memecoin supporters, but the event cannot answer the question facing thousands of ordinary holders.

A Feeling of Déjà Vu As Crypto Exchanges Fall Short in Anthropic’s IPO Tokenization
description:
This year produced the two largest IPOs in history, SpaceX in June and Anthropic on Thursday. In both cases, crypto’s attempt to give retail investors tokenized access to hot IPOs ran into the same immovable constraint. Someone still has to secure the shares.
Major crypto platforms, including Binance and Bitget, were forced to refund customers after failing to obtain enough of the underlying stock to meet tokenized-subscription demand.
London's trading industry is coming home!
High Demand, Scarce Shares
When Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei rang NASDAQ’s opening bell on November 19, the AI powerhouse began trading under ticker ANT at $111.50 per share, a swift 34% jump over its $83 IPO price.
That very day, Binance Wallet announced it would return all USDC locked in its Anthropic xStocks campaign. Run alongside xStocks, the tokenized-equity arm linked to Kraken’s parent company Payward, the campaign hit its 500 million USDC cap almost immediately before shutting down early on November 18.

Due to circumstances outside of our control, the allocation for the Anthropic xStocks IPO Campaign on Binance Wallet was not ideal. 

🔸All participating users’ USDC will be fully returned from the relevant smart contract to their Binance Wallet.

🔸 An allocation totaling roughly 2,957 Anthropic tokenized stocks, will be airdropped pro rata, based on each user's share of the total subscription, to their Binance Wallet addresses at no cost.

🔸 In addition, $1,000,000 worth of bStocks Anthropic tokens (ANTB) will be airdropped to users who applied for a subscription, with a minimum of about 6 USDC worth guaranteed for each eligible participant, and the remainder distributed pro rata based on each user's share of the total subscription.

Thank you for your patience and support. For more details, please refer to the announcement👇
https://t.co/kYf06cppeQ
— Binance Wallet (@BinanceWallet) November 19, 2026
Binance acquired a meager 2,957 tokenized shares. Rather than attempting a standard paid distribution with such tiny inventory, Binance chose to airdrop the tokens for free pro-rata to participants, fully refunding all locked USDC and tacking on $1 million in ANTB (its separate bStocks token) as compensation.
Binance Wallet cited unspecified "circumstances outside of our control" for the shortfall, admitting the tiny allocation was "not ideal." It nearly verbatim repeated Binance’s statement when its SpaceX tokenized offering collapsed back in June.
Echoes of the SpaceX Stumble
The parallels to the SpaceX fallout are hard to miss. During that launch, Binance Wallet, Bybit, Bitget Wallet and MEXC all had to pull their tokenized offerings after xStocks failed to secure enough underlying equity. Binance alone returned roughly $557 million in USDC to around 27,700 users without delivering any actual SpaceX exposure.
This time, though, at least one platform appeared to have learned a lesson about supply.

UPDATE: All the refund has been completed, as well as the rToken distribution. 

Please check your Bitget account accordingly and reach out to our support team if any queries.

Thank you all for your patience.
— Bitget (@bitget) November 20, 2026
Bypassing xStocks completely, Bitget routed its Anthropic offering through Bitget IPO Prime, its proprietary real-world-asset launchpad. By securing 153,774 shares directly, Bitget actually fulfilled user requests instead of canceling the event outright.
Bybit and MEXC sidestepped the headache altogether, avoiding asset-backed tokenized IPO deals this round.
For their part, xStocks and Kraken did not publicly disclose how many shares they secured or what share of user requests they filled. In a November 19 statement, xStocks cited oversubscription of more than 9x and confirmed that it could fulfill only part of demand.
It is worth mentioning that these episodes also highlight regulatory boundaries, as platforms like xStocks explicitly block U.S. residents from participating.
Supply, Not Demand, Remains the Bottleneck 
Ultimately, both mega-IPOs proved that retail appetite for tokenized pre-IPO access is massive, yet real-world equity sourcing remains a glaring weakness.
In the SpaceX campaign, a major failure point was xStocks, as Binance and its peers were not sourcing SpaceX shares themselves, but reselling an allocation that xStocks had promised to procure. When the supplier came up short, the reseller was inevitably left stranded. 
Bitget’s experience, though, shows that even when a platform secures shares through its own channels, retail allocation can still be vanishingly small. A tokenized IPO product is only as valuable as the shares, or economic exposure, actually behind it.


This article was written by Adonis Adoni at www.financemagnates.com.

Nvidia’s latest results should have given investors plenty of reasons to remain optimistic, yet its shares continued falling as Wall Street questioned the sustainability of the AI investment boom. Jensen Huang’s sudden departure was just one layer of uncertainty.

The company reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year. Data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, displaying a huge demand for its AI processors. Nvidia also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. Yet its shares dropped another 3.3% at the market close, extending their losing streak to six sessions.

The financial commitments behind the AI boom are also attracting greater scrutiny. Major technology companies are increasingly relying on debt markets to finance infrastructure expansion.

The European Central Bank’s November Financial Stability Review underscored growing interconnections between AI companies, including circular financing arrangements. It also warned that changing expectations around AI profitability are triggering a sharp repricing across financial markets.

title: Hyperliquid’s US Route Runs Through Regulated Firms
description:
Key Takeaways Selig cited Backpack, not Hyperliquid, as the model Backpack won separate exchange and clearing approvals ICE’s Hyperliquid plan […]
The post Hyperliquid’s US Route Runs Through Regulated Firms appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Selig cited Backpack, not Hyperliquid, as the model
  • Backpack won separate exchange and clearing approvals
  • ICE’s Hyperliquid plan still awaits regulatory sign-off
  • US traders would reach selected markets through brokers

Selig spoke at the Capitol Crypto Forum on November 19. According to The Block’s report, he answered a question about Hyperliquid by talking about onchain platforms in general, not the network itself.

What Selig Said, and What He Left Out

His answer came down to two choices: “partner with an exchange or obtain your own exchange.” Platforms could keep their onchain technology, he said, but would follow the same rules as any other exchange. He gave no timeline, mentioned no application, and said nothing about Hyperliquid’s own plans.

That leaves the starting point unchanged. Hyperliquid’s interface excludes US persons under its terms of use. So does Trade[XYZ], the largest deployer of real-world-asset markets on the network, whose official disclaimer bars United States persons from its markets. Selig’s answer did not change that. It described who would have to hold the licences before anything changes.

Backpack Is the Template He Pointed To

The example Selig cited had just cleared the CFTC. The Block reports that Backpack obtained three licences for its US entry: futures commission merchant, designated contract market and derivatives clearing organization. Two of those approvals appear in the regulator’s public records. TLD Clearing, Inc., doing business as Backpack Clearing, was registered as a clearinghouse on November 13, with permission to clear margined futures, fully collateralized futures, options on futures and swaps. Its exchange counterpart, TLD Markets, Inc., was designated on November 16.

On November 16, Selig also issued a statement welcoming the approval of exchange and clearing applications from a firm that uses blockchain-based architecture to execute and settle derivatives. The statement does not name the firm, but it was issued the same day TLD Markets was designated. Its central point is that the Commodity Exchange Act sets core principles without prescribing a technology. Firms built on a blockchain still need anti-money-laundering programs, customer protection and segregation, market surveillance, financial resources, risk management and system safeguards. The statement adds that blockchain-specific issues may need separate attention.

That is the first of Selig’s two routes in practice. Backpack did not get a ruling that its technology is acceptable. It got separate licences for each regulated job, and each licence carries its own obligations.

ICE Is Testing the Partnership Route on Hyperliquid

The second route already has a Hyperliquid-specific candidate. On October 29, Intercontinental Exchange and Trade[XYZ] announced a plan for a dedicated retail market and clearing structure built on Hyperliquid. ICE would be the exclusive operator and supply the exchange and clearing infrastructure. Trade[XYZ] would design the products, and Hyperliquid would provide the underlying infrastructure. ICE is also taking a minority stake in Trade[XYZ], and the business would sit apart from its institutional futures franchise.

The product list is broad: perpetual futures on crypto, equities, commodities, currencies and other real-world assets. Coindoo covered the announcement when it landed. What matters now is how it maps onto Selig’s answer. Backpack built its own licensed stack, while Trade[XYZ] would bring its markets to a firm that already runs regulated exchanges and clearinghouses.

Nothing is approved yet. ICE says the new market and clearing structure needs regulatory approval, including for leveraged trading. The ICE-OKX joint venture, which would route OKX’s retail customers to the markets, has its own broker-dealer and FCM approvals pending. The announcement gives no launch date.

What an American Trader Would Actually Touch

Offshore Hyperliquid markets today

Entry: a self-custody wallet connected to an interface

Eligibility: set by the interface’s terms and geoblocking

Losses beyond margin: handled by the protocol’s own liquidation mechanics

The proposed ICE market

Entry: an account at an FCM that is a platform member

Eligibility: identity and anti-money-laundering checks before trading

Losses beyond margin: backed by a CFTC-regulated clearinghouse

The trader would never deal with Hyperliquid directly. Orders and collateral would go to a broker, and the blockchain would sit underneath as the trading layer. The broker answers to the CFTC’s customer-funds rules. The exchange’s rulebook decides which contracts list. The clearinghouse decides what happens when a position fails. The CFTC’s own description of clearing covers netting obligations and transferring or mutualizing credit risk, which an onchain liquidation engine does not do on its own.

Two limits follow from that structure. First, access would cover only the contracts ICE lists, not the hundreds of markets live elsewhere on the network. Second, approving a wallet would not be enough. As Coindoo’s piece on permissioned perpetual markets set out, address controls only cover one layer. Under the ICE plan, the regulated broker carries the eligibility check.

The product type is no longer the main obstacle. In May, the CFTC allowed a CFTC-registered exchange to list a true bitcoin perpetual and granted Coinbase no-action relief tied to offshore perpetuals. US regulators have already accepted contracts with no expiry. What remains open for a Hyperliquid-based market is the structure around them and how much leverage retail customers can use.

READ MORE:

Ripple Bets on Rules Over CLARITY: Where That Falls Short

The Filings That Would Turn the Plan Into a Market

Backpack’s approvals show what completion looks like: named entities, dates and permitted activities listed on the CFTC’s website. For the ICE and Trade[XYZ] structure, the equivalent record would include:

  • CFTC approval of the new retail exchange and clearing structure, including the terms for leveraged trading
  • Broker-dealer and FCM registration for the ICE-OKX joint venture
  • Named FCMs signed up as platform members
  • Published contract specifications and a rulebook covering margin, funding payments, withdrawals and disputes

Until those records exist, the ICE plan is a proposal. Selig set out the two ways a Hyperliquid-based market can reach US customers, and Backpack has completed one of them. The CFTC’s records will show whether a Hyperliquid-based market follows.

title: Ripple Bets on Rules Over CLARITY: Where That Falls Short
description:
Key Takeaways SEC proposal could ease token fundraising rules CFTC plan covers leveraged retail crypto trades Spot-market oversight still needs […]
The post Ripple Bets on Rules Over CLARITY: Where That Falls Short appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • SEC proposal could ease token fundraising rules
  • CFTC plan covers leveraged retail crypto trades
  • Spot-market oversight still needs an act of Congress
  • Customer bankruptcy protections require statutory change

Speaking at The Hill and The Block’s Capitol Crypto Forum on November 19, Chief Legal Officer Stuart Alderoty said the focus of crypto policy will move to the SEC and CFTC, and that agency action is enough for the next two years, according to The Block’s report.

Why Ripple Is Betting on Regulators, Not Congress

Alderoty’s case rests on durability. “This administration is doing the hard work of rulemaking, and that is durable,” he said, contrasting the current approach with the SEC under Gary Gensler. In his view, rules built through public comment would be hard for a future administration to reverse.

Ripple has reason to care about that. The company spent more than four years fighting an SEC enforcement case filed in December 2020, so its legal chief has seen firsthand how the agency’s stance on crypto can shift with its leadership.

He sees the legislative route as narrower. The Block reports that Senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most prominent critics, is expected to lead the Senate Banking Committee. Alderoty said he doesn’t believe she will set crypto policy and expects her to concentrate on oversight hearings. He also doesn’t expect a version of CLARITY to be reintroduced in the next Congress, citing a crowded calendar and the 2028 presidential race, though he said parts of it could be attached to tax or other bills.

The bill has already stalled once this session: a September 15 procedural vote failed to advance it, as Coindoo reported. Any bill still pending when the current Congress ends on January 3, 2027, has to be reintroduced and start again. That is the step Alderoty doesn’t expect.

His claim that rules are enough can be tested against the two proposals regulators have already published. Each helps a different part of the market, and each stops at a different point.

For Token Issuers, the SEC Offers a New Fundraising Path

The SEC’s Regulation Crypto Assets proposal, issued August 18, would create two exemptions from Securities Act registration for certain offerings involving crypto assets: one for up to $5 million over four years, and another for up to $75 million in each 12-month period. Issuers would provide principles-based disclosures instead of a full registration statement, and the securities laws’ anti-fraud and anti-manipulation provisions would still apply.

Today, a project selling tokens as part of an investment contract must register the offering or fit into general-purpose exemptions such as Regulation D or Regulation A, none of which were written with tokens in mind. The proposal would give smaller and mid-sized raises a route built for them.

The proposal’s second element deals with what happens after the sale. It includes a conditional safe harbor from the term “investment contract,” the part of the definition of a security at the centre of most crypto enforcement cases. An arrangement that meets the conditions would fall outside that definition, which affects whether the token can later trade as something other than a security. The SEC’s summary page does not set out those conditions, so the number of projects that could rely on it will only be clear from the full text.

The proposal does not set registration rules for the platforms where tokens trade. Its comment period closed on October 20, and it stays a proposal until the Commission votes on a final version.

For Trading Platforms, the CFTC’s Reach Starts With Leverage

The CFTC’s October 13 Federal Register notice outlines two linked proposals. Regulation CTX would identify which crypto transactions the agency believes fall under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Regulation CAM would adapt the requirements for exchange-traded futures to those transactions.

Section 2(c)(2)(D), added by the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, covers commodity transactions offered to retail customers (anyone who isn’t an eligible contract participant or eligible commercial entity) on a leveraged, margined or financed basis. The financing can come from the seller, the counterparty or someone acting with either of them, so a platform that only arranges credit can still be covered. The law treats these transactions as if they were futures.

Take a platform that lets retail customers buy bitcoin with borrowed money. Unless the coins are actually delivered to the customer within 28 days, which is the statute’s main exception, the platform generally cannot offer that product unless the trades are conducted on or subject to the rules of a designated contract market. Calling it a spot purchase does not change that. The CFTC withdrew its 2020 guidance on what counts as actual delivery in December 2025, which leaves Regulation CTX’s list of covered transactions doing much of the work.

The two agencies’ proposals meet at one point. Securities are excluded from Section 2(c)(2)(D), so the SEC’s line on what counts as an investment contract helps decide which tokens the CFTC framework can reach at all.

An ordinary, unleveraged purchase sits outside this framework. For those trades, the CFTC can pursue fraud and manipulation, but it does not register or supervise the platforms. CLARITY would have changed that. A Congressional Research Service analysis of the September draft describes exclusive CFTC jurisdiction over cash and spot sales of digital commodities, with mandatory registration for the exchanges, brokers and dealers operating in those markets.

The CFTC notice is an advance notice, and comments are due December 14. A proposed rule, and then a final one, would still have to follow. Coindoo covered the plan’s earlier White House review.

Terms used in this article

ANPRM
An advance notice of proposed rulemaking. It asks for public input before an agency drafts rule text and creates no binding requirements.
Designated contract market
An exchange registered with the CFTC to list futures, subject to its rules on trading, surveillance and customer protection.
Eligible contract participant
Mainly institutions and wealthy investors. For individuals, generally more than $10 million invested on a discretionary basis, or $5 million when hedging risk.
Stockbroker liquidation
A Bankruptcy Code process in which customers share a pool of customer property ahead of a failed broker’s general creditors.

For Customers, Bankruptcy Treatment Still Needs Congress

The same CRS analysis points to a change no agency rule can make. The draft would amend the Bankruptcy Code’s stockbroker-liquidation provisions so that holders of digital assets are treated as customers, their assets are counted as customer property, and intermediaries generally cannot commingle customer assets with their own funds.

Today, a crypto customer’s position in an exchange or lender bankruptcy can turn on the platform’s terms of service. In the Celsius case, a federal bankruptcy judge ruled in January 2023 that assets in the lender’s Earn program belonged to the bankruptcy estate rather than to the customers who deposited them, leaving those customers as unsecured creditors.

Regulators can impose custody and segregation requirements on the firms they supervise. They cannot change how a bankruptcy court classifies customer assets once a firm fails. That requires an amendment to the statute.

READ MORE:

SEC Nominee Johnson Backs Full Tokenized-Stock Rules

Are Agency Rules Durable? The SEC Chair Has Doubts

Alderoty’s durability argument has a prominent skeptic: the head of one of the two agencies he is counting on. In his August statement supporting Regulation Crypto Assets, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins called legislation indispensable to lasting rules, saying it guards the SEC’s work from being “unwound by a future rogue regulator,” and pledged continued support for CLARITY.

Two separate risks sit behind that concern. The first is political. A final rule can be repealed or rewritten through the same notice-and-comment process that created it. That takes time and a supporting record, which is Alderoty’s point, but it is not out of reach. Guidance is easier to drop than a rule, yet the CFTC’s withdrawal of its own 2020 actual-delivery guidance shows how an agency’s reading of the same provision can change under new leadership.

The second risk is judicial. In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the Supreme Court held in 2024 that courts must decide for themselves whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, rather than defer to the agency’s reading of an ambiguous statute. The SEC’s safe harbor is the clearest test case. “Investment contract” is a statutory term the Supreme Court has interpreted since its 1946 Howey decision, so anyone challenging the rule could ask a court whether the SEC’s line matches the statute, and the court would answer that question without deferring to the agency.

Put together, the agency route offers the most to token issuers, a defined but narrow path to platforms offering leveraged trades, and the least to customers worried about what happens if a platform fails. Alderoty says that is enough for the next two years. Atkins, whose agency wrote one of the two proposals, is still asking Congress for the rest.

The post Ripple Bets on Rules Over CLARITY: Where That Falls Short appeared first on Coindoo.

title: ETH Longs Eat $11.25M as Price Slides to $1,745
description:

The post ETH Longs Eat $11.25M as Price Slides to $1,745 appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
ETH longs took $11.25M in ethereum liquidations. Spot slid to $1,745 in that same hour. Aggregated force-close tallies from Binance, Bybit, and OKX logged the wipeout through 21:20 UTC on November 19, 2026. Total liquidations on those venues reached about $11.46 million. Price fell about 1.13% from $1,764 to $1,745. Leveraged bulls cleared as Ethereum broke under $1,750.

Why Ethereum Liquidations Hit Longs First

Long liquidations were $11.25 million of the $11.46 million total. Short liquidations came to only about $210,000 on the same three venues. This means the flush hit longs almost exclusively. In other words, the window was a one-sided ethereum liquidations event, not a balanced squeeze.

Binance ETHUSDT printed the slide in the same hour. The 21:00 UTC candle opened at $1,761.20. It closed at $1,741.60 after a session low of $1,736.28. The 21:20 UTC minute close sat near $1,745.16. That print matched the $1,745 handle in the venue tally. Spot quote volume on that flush hour ran near $37 million on Binance. The Motley Fool listed Ether at $1,745.57 in its early-evening tape. The 24-hour decline was about 1.64%. This means two separate prints landed on the same sub-$1,750 zone.

The $1,764 starting print sits above the Binance hour open of $1,761.20. The $1,745 finish sits above the $1,736.28 session low. This means the ethereum liquidations clock covered the slide into $1,745. Binance still tagged a deeper wick inside the same hour. In other words, the force-close level and the deepest spot print are related but not identical.

What Traders Watch After $1,745

The base number is the $11.25 million long wipeout. The fuller venue total is $11.46 million once shorts of $210,000 are added. This means about $210,000 sits outside the long side. Almost nothing else remains from that hour's force-closes on Binance, Bybit, and OKX. Holders now treat $1,745 as the named ethereum liquidations mark from the three-exchange tally. They treat $1,736.28 as the deepest Binance tag from the same hour. A reclaim above $1,760 would pull price away from the force-close print. A slip back under $1,745 keeps that flush level in play after the wick to $1,736.28. The wider risk is another break under that band. Fresh longs that reload too close to the same floor can feed a second round of liquidations.

The post ETH Longs Eat $11.25M as Price Slides to $1,745 appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.

Binance ETHUSDT closed the 21:00 UTC hour at $1,741.60 after a flush that tagged $1,736.28. The next hour opened at that $1,741 handle. It then pushed through $1,762 by about […]
The post Ethereum Price Rebound Lifts ETH 1.2% to $1,762 appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
An ethereum price rebound lifted ETH about 1.2% in one hour to near $1,762. The spot pair had just printed a $1,741 dip on Binance. Binance ETHUSDT closed the 21:00 UTC hour at $1,741.60 after a flush that tagged $1,736.28. The next hour opened at that $1,741 handle. It then pushed through $1,762 by about 22:35 UTC. The bounce forced about $690,000 in short liquidations across major venues. The reclaim still held near $1,760 into the following prints.

Why the Ethereum Price Rebound Stuck

The 22:00 UTC Binance hour opened at $1,741.61 and closed at $1,760.52. The high of that hour was $1,766.39. This means buyers lifted the pair about $19 off the hour open. The print then settled just under $1,761. In other words, the move was a timed spot rebound from the $1,741 dip. It was not a slow grind across a full session. CoinGecko minute prints showed ETH near $1,762 around 22:40 UTC. That matched the same reclaim window. Later readings still sat near $1,760. About a 1.1% hourly gain remained visible on the bounce candle. The reclaim therefore stuck after the flush. It did not fade back into the $1,745 area on the first retest.

Short liquidations of about $690,000 hit during that rebound hour. Those totals came from major venues that publish aggregated force-close figures. This means leveraged shorts paid when price jumped from the $1,741 open toward $1,762. Binance futures open interest on ETHUSDT slipped during the flush hour. It then rebuilt as the spot pair reclaimed. Funding on the Binance ETHUSDT perpetual stayed near flat at about 0.005% per period after the bounce. In other words, the tape showed a short squeeze of limited size. It was not a broad leverage reset.

What Traders Watch After $1,762

The session low on Binance was $1,736.28 inside the 21:00 UTC hour. The close of that hour was $1,741.60. This means the deepest print sat under the $1,741 handle that later became the bounce open. Spot volume on that flush hour ran near $37 million in quote terms on Binance ETHUSDT. The rebound hour still cleared about $20 million. Holders watching the Ethereum pair now treat $1,741 as the flush close. They treat $1,762 as the first reclaim mark. A slip back under $1,745 would erase the hourly gain that defined this rebound. Prior ETH dips below $2,100 showed how fast support can fail. A hold above $1,760 keeps the bounce intact after the $1,741 dip. The next test is whether ETH can defend that zone on quieter volume. The first push was funded by the liquidation burst.
