title: Could Bitcoin’s March 2020 Crash Repeat?
Bitcoin Optech Newsletter #432
description:
This week’s newsletter summarizes an analysis of decentralized mining pool
payouts, describes the disclosure of a fixed denial-of-service vulnerability
in Eclair, and links to continued discussion about whether stale tip relay
should include block data. Also included are our regular sections describing
recent changes to services and client software, announcing new releases and
release candidates, and describing notable changes to popular Bitcoin
infrastructure software.
News
● Framework for decentralized mining pool payouts: Developer 7d5x9
posted to Delving Bitcoin an analysis of how decentralized
mining pools can pay miners directly from coinbase
transactions, which the post calls decentralized coinbase payout protocols
(DCPPs). Giving every miner its own output does not scale because mining
firmware limits coinbase transaction size and each output displaces
fee-paying transactions. The post argues that when a pool has more miners
than outputs, any rule ranking miners by work allows a rich list attack,
where a large miner splits its hashrate across identities that each still
outrank the smallest miners, pushing them out of the coinbase transaction.
According to 7d5x9, earlier designs only move this problem. Braidpool shifts
it from who receives an output to who controls the pool’s threshold key (see
Newsletter #340). For a single coinbase output paying a
joinpool with unilateral exits, the obstacle is that
miners vary the coinbase transaction for extra nonce space, so its txid is
unknown and exit transactions cannot be signed until a block is found. 7d5x9
believes this leaves the output controlled by a single key or threshold of
keys until a soft fork enables rebindable signatures, such as those proposed
in BIP448 (see Newsletter #397). In sketches based on
Spark-style statechains and on Ark, an
attacker keeping one small claim per subtree can block cheap cooperative
settlement, raising miners’ costs, though the post considers this less
severe for Ark.
The post concludes that a joinpool does not decide which outputs enter the
coinbase transaction. It sees two options for that: a value-weighted random
draw (an idea credited to Matt Corallo) or outputs reserved for designated
operators.
LearnBitcoin.com, who ran a public P2Pool node, examined 2,545
P2Pool coinbase transactions and argued that growth alone, without any
attacker, squeezed out small miners because P2Pool raised the share
difficulty of miners expected to earn under 0.001 BTC per block. For its
successor P2Poolv2, jungly suggested a limit of 16 outputs
given current firmware. Steven Roose replied that he could not
think of a scheme worth exploring without covenants,
which would let a coinbase output deterministically commit to an Ark
transaction tree that pays every miner who uses the same Ark server.
● Disclosure of a DoS vulnerability in Eclair: rorp posted
to Delving Bitcoin the responsible disclosure of a memory-exhaustion denial-of-service (DoS)
vulnerability affecting Eclair version 0.14.0 and fixed in July
2026 in release 0.14.1. Any peer able to connect to a vulnerable node could crash
it, even without having a channel with it. The bug gave an attacker no
direct access to funds, but repeatedly crashing a node could put its channel
funds at risk. Users still running 0.14.0 should upgrade.
The attack vector leveraged a missing size check in Eclair. According to BOLT2,
messages can be sent in batches to be treated as a single logical update through the
start_batch message, which among other fields carries the batch_size. According
to the specifications, the size must be at most 20 and strictly greater than 1.
While Eclair checked for the upper bound, it did not enforce the lower one.
An attacker would have been able to use this vulnerability by sending a start_batch
message with batch_size = 0, followed by commitment_signed messages, which are
sent in batches during splicing. Since the code stopped adding
messages to its internal batch only once the number of received messages reached the
batch_size (which was 0, thus always lower than the number of messages received),
the list never stopped growing, leading to memory exhaustion.
The vulnerability was fixed by having the code check the lower bound, too, as
specified in BOLT2.
● Continued discussion of stale tip relay: Antoine Poinsot
replied to the Bitcoin-Dev mailing list thread about
BIP332 stale tip relay (see Newsletters #417 and
#423) to suggest that nodes initially relay only the
headers of stale blocks. Poinsot argued that headers are enough to make stale
blocks observable. Relaying the block data as well lets nodes reorganize
faster to a chain built on a stale block, which increases the expected
revenue of a miner that briefly keeps mining on its own block after losing a
block race. Poinsot considered that effect most likely
small but not worth working out rigorously.
Anthony Towns replied that any miner who would benefit can
cheaply implement stale block relay itself. Towns
estimated that a pool with 20% of network hashrate already
gains about 16.1 BTC per year by mining on its own block instead of a
competing block it saw first at the same height, and that cutting the relay
delay of the resulting one-block reorg from five seconds to one would raise
that to 16.36 BTC. Towns also argued that stale headers can raise concerns,
such as possible selfish mining, but only the block
data can settle them. Poinsot agreed that the estimate
appears to cover the effect on honest mining incentives and, while still
seeing most of the value in headers, did not want to block relaying full
blocks.
Changes to services and client software
In this monthly feature, we highlight interesting updates to Bitcoin
wallets and services.
● Liana v16.0 released: Liana v16.0 writes its encrypted
descriptor backups in the BIP138 format (see
Newsletter #424) and makes taproot the
default for new wallets.
● COLDCARD firmware adds codex32 backups: Coinkite
announced COLDCARD firmware versions 5.6.3 and 1.5.3Q,
which add support for generating and importing codex32
secrets and for splitting the device’s wallet into two to nine Shamir shares
for later recovery. The releases also add support for per-input height and
time locktimes in PSBTv2 transactions.
● Wavelength released on mainnet: Lightning Labs
announced that Wavelength, its Ark-like
payments toolkit (see Newsletter #415), is available
on mainnet as an alpha with accounts limited to 300,000 sats.
● Bull Bitcoin makes payjoin the default for exchange orders: Bull Bitcoin
announced that onchain purchases and sales made on its
exchange through the Bull Bitcoin Mobile wallet now use
payjoin by default (see Newsletter #338).
Version 6.14.0 of the wallet also adds experimental support
for sending and receiving silent payments.
● Breez SDK adds silent payment sending: Version 0.28.0 of
the Spark-based Breez SDK adds support for sending to
silent payment addresses.
● Silent payments scanner for Electrum plugin: Ali Sherief
announced spscand, a watch-only
silent payments scanner that works with the
Electrum sending plugin covered in Newsletter #419.
It can scan for payments using the user’s own Bitcoin Core node, a BlindBit
server, or a BlindBit server combined with
compact block filters from P2P peers.
● Stratum v2 releases and pool adoption: The
Stratum v2 reference implementation released
sv2-apps v0.9.0, which adds support for Bitcoin Core 32.x, including
submitting found blocks over its IPC interface, and hardens its Job
Declarator Client (see Newsletter #384 for previous
coverage). Separately, MARA Foundation announced that MARA mined
its first block using Stratum v2, and Foundry announced that
it has begun testing Stratum v2 on its pool.
● Coinswap renamed to OpenSwap: OpenSwap v0.2.3 is the first release
under the new name of the coinswap protocol implementation
formerly called Coinswap (see Newsletter #415). It adds
an Electrum server backend option, swaps that pay a third-party address,
and, when built with Lightning support, swaps between onchain funds and LN
through LDK Server (see Newsletter #406).
Releases and release candidates
New releases and release candidates for popular Bitcoin infrastructure
projects.  Please consider upgrading to new releases or helping to test
release candidates.
● Core Lightning 26.12rc1 is a release candidate for the next major version
of this popular LN node implementation. It will be the first major release
since 26.06 and covers two release cycles. It adds a tool for recovering
HTLC outputs after channel-state loss (see Core Lightning #9730
below), improves payment pathfinding (see Newsletters #418 and #430), and adds experimental support for a
new cooperative close protocol (see Newsletter #413).
The release notes also announce that xpay will replace pay in 27.03.
Notable code and documentation changes
Notable recent changes in Bitcoin Core, Core
Lightning, Eclair, LDK,
LND, libsecp256k1, Hardware Wallet
Interface (HWI), Rust Bitcoin, BTCPay
Server, BDK, Bitcoin Improvement
Proposals (BIPs), Lightning BOLTs,
Lightning BLIPs, Bitcoin Inquisition, and BINANAs.
● Bitcoin Core #36757 fixes a privacy leak in address discovery over Tor
and I2P. Previously, when a node connected
outbound to a malicious Tor or I2P peer, that peer could claim to see the
node at an arbitrary routable IP address in its version message. Bitcoin
Core could then advertise that address back to the peer, along with its own
clearnet listening port. A distinctive port could then help correlate the
connection with a clearnet node that was observed using the same port (see
Newsletter #52 for an earlier Tor listening-port fix). Bitcoin
Core now ignores the address that Tor and I2P peers report seeing the
node at.
● BIPs #2356 replaces the placeholder genesis parameters in BIP95 with
those of the mined testnet5 genesis block and marks the BIP
as Deployed. The genesis coinbase includes the date 2026-11-14 and the hash
of mainnet block 975,744. Committing to that hash ensures that the testnet5
genesis block could only be mined after mainnet reached that height (see
Newsletter #431).
● Core Lightning #9730 adds the lightning-hsmtool recoverhtlc command to
manually recover HTLC outputs after local channel-state loss.
Once the peer publishes its latest commitment transaction, the recovering
node can already reclaim its main output using a static channel
backup (see Newsletter #421). Given the local hsm_secret, channel and HTLC details, and the
peer’s per-commitment point, the new command identifies matching HTLC
outputs. The tool constructs signed transactions to reclaim outgoing HTLCs
after a timeout or to claim incoming HTLCs with known preimages. However, the
operator must manually review and broadcast the transactions. A cooperative
CLN peer can export the public point using the
dumpcommitments --point-only command without revealing secrets.
● LDK #5561 fixes a potential loss of forwarded funds when a peer sends
revoke_and_ack before LDK sends the corresponding commitment_signed
message. Previously, LDK could accept this premature acknowledgment and
advance its internal commitment number. Consequently, it could sign a
commitment that differed from the one recorded by its onchain monitor. If the
peer published that commitment, LDK might fail to claim the incoming HTLC,
even after paying the outgoing HTLC, despite knowing its preimage. LDK now
rejects the premature acknowledgment and force closes the channel. The fix
was released in LDK 0.2.8 (see Newsletter #431). Newsletter
#426 described an earlier bug that left a signed commitment
unmonitored during reconnection.
● LDK #5562 and #5545 fix channel ID collisions that a
malicious peer could create between its channels and an LDK node. In the
first, the peer could reuse a force-closed channel’s known ID as a new
channel’s temporary ID. This could prevent LDK from recording a forwarded
payment’s preimage in the closed channel’s monitor, leaving the incoming
HTLC unclaimed after the outgoing HTLC had been paid. In the
second, the peer could calculate a channel’s future final ID from its funding
transaction and submit another opening request with that temporary ID. If the
original channel adopted its final ID before the application accepted the new
request, acceptance could overwrite its funded state. LDK now rejects
conflicting IDs and rechecks them at acceptance. Both fixes were also
released in LDK 0.2.8. See Newsletter #427 for related
channel ID collisions that could cause a DoS in Eclair.
● LDK #5557 fixes a vulnerability that allowed malicious peers to disrupt
transaction monitoring on nodes using an Electrum backend. The peer could
propose a channel whose claimed funding output reused an already-watched
outpoint, but with a different locking script. Registering that proposal
could overwrite the legitimate watch’s stored script, even if LDK
subsequently rejected the channel. LDK would then query Electrum for
transactions associated with the bogus script and might miss a transaction
spending the real output, preventing a timely response to a channel closure.
LDK now retains every distinct script registered for an outpoint, so a bogus
registration cannot suppress the legitimate watch. This fix was also released
in LDK 0.2.8.
● LDK #5558 and #5482 fix two ways payments could exceed their
fee budget. The first PR addresses the handling of an omitted fee-limit
setting for async payments using static
BOLT12 invoices (see Newsletter #321). LDK
now applies its default cap of 1% of the payment amount plus 50 sat when the
application omits the setting. Previously, omitting it removed the limit
entirely, allowing a malicious receiver to supply a blinded path with excessive fees. This fix was also released in LDK 0.2.8. The
second PR addresses retries when a route adds value to meet an HTLC minimum.
LDK treated the extra value as part of the requested payment and restored the
failed path’s fee budget on retry, allowing the total spend to exceed its
limit. LDK now retries only the remaining amount owed and counts any excess
against the remaining fee budget.
● LND #11555 changes how LND reports non-AMP invoices as
settled. Although applications could already monitor when the settlement of
individual HTLCs was locked in offchain (see Newsletter
#224), LND could mark an invoice as settled as soon as the
preimage was released. The invoice now enters the PENDING_SETTLE state on
preimage release. Once every HTLC in the payment has a final offchain or
onchain outcome, LND marks the invoice as SETTLED if all parts were
collected or CANCELED if any failed. A canceled invoice can still have
collected some parts, which are not refunded, so applications should credit
only the amounts from finalized, successful HTLCs. An invoice’s
preimage_released flag records whether LND has committed to releasing the
preimage. AMP payment sets still settle at preimage release.
● LND #11551 fixes expiry validation when completing multipath
payments and AMP payments.
Previously, LND checked each HTLC when it arrived. If more blocks were mined
while the receiver waited for the remaining parts, LND could release
preimages even though an earlier HTLC no longer had the required expiry
margin for onchain collection. Now, LND rechecks
every part against the current block height when the final part arrives. If a
previously accepted part is now too close to expiry, LND fails that set and
leaves the invoice open for another attempt (see Newsletter #424 for earlier work on canceling individual AMP sets).
● LND #11472 and #10842 fix cases where temporary backend
errors or one problematic input could block otherwise valid sweeps. The first
keeps inputs available for retry after temporary or unclassified errors
during mempool acceptance checks (see Newsletter #373). It
was released in LND 0.21.8-beta and 0.20.8-beta (see Newsletter
#431). The second uses diagnostic transactions that are never
broadcast to test subsets of a rejected batch. If an invalid or conflicting
input can be identified, LND excludes it from the next attempt and retries
the remaining inputs.
● LND #11542 fixes recovery of forwarded HTLCs after channel
reconnections. When replaying stored forwarding batches, LND could filter out
acknowledged HTLCs and then use the remaining entries’ new positions to look
up metadata indexed by their original positions. This could cause unresolved
HTLCs to be skipped or misassociated. Additionally, if a channel’s HTLC
handler stopped after LND recorded the batch but before handing off an HTLC,
an incomplete record could be left behind, causing retries to be discarded as
duplicates. LND now preserves the original batch indexes and removes
incomplete records after a failed handoff, allowing unresolved HTLCs to be
retried. The fix was released in LND 0.21.8-beta and 0.20.8-beta (see
Newsletter #431).
Want more?
For more discussion about the topics mentioned in this newsletter, join us for
the weekly Bitcoin Optech Recap on Riverside.fm at
17:30 UTC on November 24.  The
discussion is also recorded and will be available from our podcasts
page.

Steven Roose replied that he could not think of a scheme worth exploring without covenants, which would let a coinbase output deterministically commit to an Ark transaction tree that pays every miner who uses the same Ark server.

  • ● Disclosure of a DoS vulnerability in Eclair: rorp posted to Delving Bitcoin the responsible disclosure of a memory-exhaustion denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability affecting Eclair version 0.14.0 and fixed in July 2026 in release 0.14.1. Any peer able to connect to a vulnerable node could crash it, even without having a channel with it. The bug gave an attacker no direct access to funds, but repeatedly crashing a node could put its channel funds at risk. Users still running 0.14.0 should upgrade.

    The attack vector leveraged a missing size check in Eclair. According to BOLT2, messages can be sent in batches to be treated as a single logical update through the start_batch message, which among other fields carries the batch_size. According to the specifications, the size must be at most 20 and strictly greater than 1. While Eclair checked for the upper bound, it did not enforce the lower one.

    An attacker would have been able to use this vulnerability by sending a start_batch message with batch_size = 0, followed by commitment_signed messages, which are sent in batches during splicing. Since the code stopped adding messages to its internal batch only once the number of received messages reached the batch_size (which was 0, thus always lower than the number of messages received), the list never stopped growing, leading to memory exhaustion. The vulnerability was fixed by having the code check the lower bound, too, as specified in BOLT2.

  • ● Continued discussion of stale tip relay: Antoine Poinsot replied to the Bitcoin-Dev mailing list thread about BIP332 stale tip relay (see Newsletters #417 and #423) to suggest that nodes initially relay only the headers of stale blocks. Poinsot argued that headers are enough to make stale blocks observable. Relaying the block data as well lets nodes reorganize faster to a chain built on a stale block, which increases the expected revenue of a miner that briefly keeps mining on its own block after losing a block race. Poinsot considered that effect most likely small but not worth working out rigorously.

    Anthony Towns replied that any miner who would benefit can cheaply implement stale block relay itself. Towns estimated that a pool with 20% of network hashrate already gains about 16.1 BTC per year by mining on its own block instead of a competing block it saw first at the same height, and that cutting the relay delay of the resulting one-block reorg from five seconds to one would raise that to 16.36 BTC. Towns also argued that stale headers can raise concerns, such as possible selfish mining, but only the block data can settle them. Poinsot agreed that the estimate appears to cover the effect on honest mining incentives and, while still seeing most of the value in headers, did not want to block relaying full blocks.

Changes to services and client software

In this monthly feature, we highlight interesting updates to Bitcoin wallets and services.

  • ● Liana v16.0 released: Liana v16.0 writes its encrypted descriptor backups in the BIP138 format (see Newsletter #424) and makes taproot the default for new wallets.

  • ● COLDCARD firmware adds codex32 backups: Coinkite announced COLDCARD firmware versions 5.6.3 and 1.5.3Q, which add support for generating and importing codex32 secrets and for splitting the device’s wallet into two to nine Shamir shares for later recovery. The releases also add support for per-input height and time locktimes in PSBTv2 transactions.

  • ● Wavelength released on mainnet: Lightning Labs announced that Wavelength, its Ark-like payments toolkit (see Newsletter #415), is available on mainnet as an alpha with accounts limited to 300,000 sats.

  • ● Bull Bitcoin makes payjoin the default for exchange orders: Bull Bitcoin announced that onchain purchases and sales made on its exchange through the Bull Bitcoin Mobile wallet now use payjoin by default (see Newsletter #338). Version 6.14.0 of the wallet also adds experimental support for sending and receiving silent payments.

  • ● Breez SDK adds silent payment sending: Version 0.28.0 of the Spark-based Breez SDK adds support for sending to silent payment addresses.

  • ● Silent payments scanner for Electrum plugin: Ali Sherief announced spscand, a watch-only silent payments scanner that works with the Electrum sending plugin covered in Newsletter #419. It can scan for payments using the user’s own Bitcoin Core node, a BlindBit server, or a BlindBit server combined with compact block filters from P2P peers.

  • ● Stratum v2 releases and pool adoption: The Stratum v2 reference implementation released sv2-apps v0.9.0, which adds support for Bitcoin Core 32.x, including submitting found blocks over its IPC interface, and hardens its Job Declarator Client (see Newsletter #384 for previous coverage). Separately, MARA Foundation announced that MARA mined its first block using Stratum v2, and Foundry announced that it has begun testing Stratum v2 on its pool.

  • ● Coinswap renamed to OpenSwap: OpenSwap v0.2.3 is the first release under the new name of the coinswap protocol implementation formerly called Coinswap (see Newsletter #415). It adds an Electrum server backend option, swaps that pay a third-party address, and, when built with Lightning support, swaps between onchain funds and LN through LDK Server (see Newsletter #406).

Releases and release candidates

New releases and release candidates for popular Bitcoin infrastructure projects. Please consider upgrading to new releases or helping to test release candidates.

  • ● Core Lightning 26.12rc1 is a release candidate for the next major version of this popular LN node implementation. It will be the first major release since 26.06 and covers two release cycles. It adds a tool for recovering HTLC outputs after channel-state loss (see Core Lightning #9730 below), improves payment pathfinding (see Newsletters #418 and #430), and adds experimental support for a new cooperative close protocol (see Newsletter #413). The release notes also announce that xpay will replace pay in 27.03.

Notable code and documentation changes

Notable recent changes in Bitcoin Core, Core Lightning, Eclair, LDK, LND, libsecp256k1, Hardware Wallet Interface (HWI), Rust Bitcoin, BTCPay Server, BDK, Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs), Lightning BOLTs, Lightning BLIPs, Bitcoin Inquisition, and BINANAs.

  • ● Bitcoin Core #36757 fixes a privacy leak in address discovery over Tor and I2P. Previously, when a node connected outbound to a malicious Tor or I2P peer, that peer could claim to see the node at an arbitrary routable IP address in its version message. Bitcoin Core could then advertise that address back to the peer, along with its own clearnet listening port. A distinctive port could then help correlate the connection with a clearnet node that was observed using the same port (see Newsletter #52 for an earlier Tor listening-port fix). Bitcoin Core now ignores the address that Tor and I2P peers report seeing the node at.

  • ● BIPs #2356 replaces the placeholder genesis parameters in BIP95 with those of the mined testnet5 genesis block and marks the BIP as Deployed. The genesis coinbase includes the date 2026-11-14 and the hash of mainnet block 975,744. Committing to that hash ensures that the testnet5 genesis block could only be mined after mainnet reached that height (see Newsletter #431).

  • ● Core Lightning #9730 adds the lightning-hsmtool recoverhtlc command to manually recover HTLC outputs after local channel-state loss. Once the peer publishes its latest commitment transaction, the recovering node can already reclaim its main output using a static channel backup (see Newsletter #421). Given the local hsm_secret, channel and HTLC details, and the peer’s per-commitment point, the new command identifies matching HTLC outputs. The tool constructs signed transactions to reclaim outgoing HTLCs after a timeout or to claim incoming HTLCs with known preimages. However, the operator must manually review and broadcast the transactions. A cooperative CLN peer can export the public point using the dumpcommitments --point-only command without revealing secrets.

  • ● LDK #5561 fixes a potential loss of forwarded funds when a peer sends revoke_and_ack before LDK sends the corresponding commitment_signed message. Previously, LDK could accept this premature acknowledgment and advance its internal commitment number. Consequently, it could sign a commitment that differed from the one recorded by its onchain monitor. If the peer published that commitment, LDK might fail to claim the incoming HTLC, even after paying the outgoing HTLC, despite knowing its preimage. LDK now rejects the premature acknowledgment and force closes the channel. The fix was released in LDK 0.2.8 (see Newsletter #431). Newsletter #426 described an earlier bug that left a signed commitment unmonitored during reconnection.

  • ● LDK #5562 and #5545 fix channel ID collisions that a malicious peer could create between its channels and an LDK node. In the first, the peer could reuse a force-closed channel’s known ID as a new channel’s temporary ID. This could prevent LDK from recording a forwarded payment’s preimage in the closed channel’s monitor, leaving the incoming HTLC unclaimed after the outgoing HTLC had been paid. In the second, the peer could calculate a channel’s future final ID from its funding transaction and submit another opening request with that temporary ID. If the original channel adopted its final ID before the application accepted the new request, acceptance could overwrite its funded state. LDK now rejects conflicting IDs and rechecks them at acceptance. Both fixes were also released in LDK 0.2.8. See Newsletter #427 for related channel ID collisions that could cause a DoS in Eclair.

  • ● LDK #5557 fixes a vulnerability that allowed malicious peers to disrupt transaction monitoring on nodes using an Electrum backend. The peer could propose a channel whose claimed funding output reused an already-watched outpoint, but with a different locking script. Registering that proposal could overwrite the legitimate watch’s stored script, even if LDK subsequently rejected the channel. LDK would then query Electrum for transactions associated with the bogus script and might miss a transaction spending the real output, preventing a timely response to a channel closure. LDK now retains every distinct script registered for an outpoint, so a bogus registration cannot suppress the legitimate watch. This fix was also released in LDK 0.2.8.

  • ● LDK #5558 and #5482 fix two ways payments could exceed their fee budget. The first PR addresses the handling of an omitted fee-limit setting for async payments using static BOLT12 invoices (see Newsletter #321). LDK now applies its default cap of 1% of the payment amount plus 50 sat when the application omits the setting. Previously, omitting it removed the limit entirely, allowing a malicious receiver to supply a blinded path with excessive fees. This fix was also released in LDK 0.2.8. The second PR addresses retries when a route adds value to meet an HTLC minimum. LDK treated the extra value as part of the requested payment and restored the failed path’s fee budget on retry, allowing the total spend to exceed its limit. LDK now retries only the remaining amount owed and counts any excess against the remaining fee budget.

  • ● LND #11555 changes how LND reports non-AMP invoices as settled. Although applications could already monitor when the settlement of individual HTLCs was locked in offchain (see Newsletter #224), LND could mark an invoice as settled as soon as the preimage was released. The invoice now enters the PENDING_SETTLE state on preimage release. Once every HTLC in the payment has a final offchain or onchain outcome, LND marks the invoice as SETTLED if all parts were collected or CANCELED if any failed. A canceled invoice can still have collected some parts, which are not refunded, so applications should credit only the amounts from finalized, successful HTLCs. An invoice’s preimage_released flag records whether LND has committed to releasing the preimage. AMP payment sets still settle at preimage release.

  • ● LND #11551 fixes expiry validation when completing multipath payments and AMP payments. Previously, LND checked each HTLC when it arrived. If more blocks were mined while the receiver waited for the remaining parts, LND could release preimages even though an earlier HTLC no longer had the required expiry margin for onchain collection. Now, LND rechecks every part against the current block height when the final part arrives. If a previously accepted part is now too close to expiry, LND fails that set and leaves the invoice open for another attempt (see Newsletter #424 for earlier work on canceling individual AMP sets).

  • ● LND #11472 and #10842 fix cases where temporary backend errors or one problematic input could block otherwise valid sweeps. The first keeps inputs available for retry after temporary or unclassified errors during mempool acceptance checks (see Newsletter #373). It was released in LND 0.21.8-beta and 0.20.8-beta (see Newsletter #431). The second uses diagnostic transactions that are never broadcast to test subsets of a rejected batch. If an invalid or conflicting input can be identified, LND excludes it from the next attempt and retries the remaining inputs.

  • ● LND #11542 fixes recovery of forwarded HTLCs after channel reconnections. When replaying stored forwarding batches, LND could filter out acknowledged HTLCs and then use the remaining entries’ new positions to look up metadata indexed by their original positions. This could cause unresolved HTLCs to be skipped or misassociated. Additionally, if a channel’s HTLC handler stopped after LND recorded the batch but before handing off an HTLC, an incomplete record could be left behind, causing retries to be discarded as duplicates. LND now preserves the original batch indexes and removes incomplete records after a failed handoff, allowing unresolved HTLCs to be retried. The fix was released in LND 0.21.8-beta and 0.20.8-beta (see Newsletter #431).

Want more?

For more discussion about the topics mentioned in this newsletter, join us for the weekly Bitcoin Optech Recap on Riverside.fm at 17:30 UTC on November 24. The discussion is also recorded and will be available from our podcasts page.

fullContent:
WASHINGTON—In a change of designation that marks a major step backward in the effort to curb rowdy youth subcultures, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced Wednesday that the United States had officially lost its greaser elimination status. “Following significant upticks in the number of defiant teens sporting slicked-back hair, leather biker jackets, and cuffed blue jeans, we must regretfully remove the U.S. from our list of greaser-free countries,” PAHO director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said in a public statement, explaining that what began with the isolated incident of a sock hop in West Texas had rapidly grown into a nationwide epidemic. “Unfortunately, as more parents have declined to raise their children to be clean-cut, the greaser infestation continues to spread undeterred through our high schools, drive-in theaters, malt shops, and vacant parking lots. Not since the rockabilly revival of the early 1980s have Americans been exposed to these staggering levels of pomade and Brylcreem. We fought long and hard to eradicate chain-smoking, finger-snapping delinquents in our country, and it will likely take decades of work to get them back under control. We urge officials to contain the outbreak by enforcing strict public dress codes and anti-loitering laws as soon as possible.” Barbosa went on to warn that if the United States continued down its current path, it could soon see a resurgence of beatniks.

The post U.S. Loses Greaser Elimination Status appeared first on The Onion.

title: Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future
On November 10, 2026, President Nayib Bukele hosted roughly 30 Bitcoiners at Casa Presidencial during Bitcoin Histórico. Guests included Ricardo Salinas Pliego, Parker Lewis, Mike Peterson, and miners; discussions covered power generation for compute and immigration.
This post Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future

This November 10, in the midst of the Bitcoin Histórico conference taking place in the Historical Center of San Salvador, a group of Bitcoiners representing a wide range of sectors within the industry met with President Bukele.

The dinner was organized by The Bitcoin Office, which is part of the Office of the President, and was led by Stacy Herbert and Max Keiser. The dinner went on from about 7:30 pm to 10:30 pm local time and included about thirty Bitcoiners, many regular visitors to El Salvador. 

Among the guests was billionaire Ricardo Salinas Pliego, founder of Grupo Salinas, which owns Banco Azteca. Salinas is a known Bitcoiner, who has made public appearances with Keiser and Herbert in the past, and is speculated to be planning a run at the next Mexican Presidential election. Salinas met privately with the President besides the dinner and reportedly gifted him volumes one and two of Manuscripts of the Conquistadors, works curated and edited by Jorge Nikaido, Chief of Staff of Grupo Salinas.

Representing investors and founders were Parker Lewis, founder of Unchained Capital, Mike Peterson of Bitcoin Beach fame, Katie Ananina of Citizen X, and Aleks Svetski, entrepreneur and founder of Satlantis. Bitcoin miners also attended, such as  Beau Turner,  CEO of  Abundant Mines, Nacho Pauls, CCO of OCEAN Mining, and Adam Ortolf of Denver Bitcoin mining. Jon Atack, a Bitcoin core contributor, was also at the dinner alongside engineer Giacomo Zucco of Plan B Network, and AI tech entrepreneurs Ginger Gaetz of the ANIA AI initiative and Marc Seal, Founder of Aevonix.

The academic and media side of the industry was also heavily represented, with none other than Michael Goldstein, also known as Bitstein and co-founder of the Nakamoto Institute. Eric Yakes, economist and author of The 7th Property, was there, as well as Efrat Feningson, independent journalist and podcaster. Local Bitcoiner Michael Ruiz also attended the dinner; he is the founder of Build in El Salvador (BIS), an increasingly popular kind of business club and Bitcoin meetup mix. 

Setting the Table

The guests arrived at the Casa Presidencial earlier in the evening and were chatting and networking while waiting for the president. Max Keiser, always a showman, arrived at the Casa Presidencial with a gift some might speculate carried a magical artefact. Photographed above, the case was said to contain a Stetson El Presidente cowboy hat, though some have speculated it might in fact have carried the Philosopher’s Stone. 

Upon arrival, Bukele shook everyone’s hand and quickly invited them to take their assigned seats, dine, and relax- no big speeches or over-the-top formalities, Ananina told Bitcoin Magazine, describing the dinner as a kind of open mic. 

“President Bukele’s table was adorned with bitcoin orange florals,” Herbert told Bitcoin Magazine; “we gathered anarchists, billionaire tycoons, Wall Street bankers, circular economy activists, VC investors, bitcoin miners, and content creators” at the country’s equivalent of the White House.  

A three-course meal began to be served, with steak — of course — being the main course, followed by a three-layered chocolate dessert. In between were three hours of conversation which left a very strong impression on the individuals interviewed on the night. Bukele had his own microphone, while a couple of other mics were passed around. Six to seven major questions were asked throughout the night.

Salinas and Energy Investments

At some point, energy generation came up, and Salinas in particular engaged the topic with the President. 

Baeu Turner, one of the three bitcoin miners at the dinner, told Bitcoin Magazine that Bukele described El Salvador’s electricity generation as “being roughly matched to the country’s current demand.” Bukele described plans to add more than a gigawatt of additional generation across multiple projects, including geothermal and generation using imported liquefied natural gas.

“What stood out to me,” added Turner, “was how directly he connected those development plans with demand for compute. Bukele said they can develop this power knowing there are users who can put it to work, whether that’s Bitcoin mining or other data centers. The demand could come from the Salvadoran government’s own operations or from outside companies bringing equipment and investment into the country.”

Other miners responded positively to that idea, including Salinas, who has deep investments and experience with energy production. His Grupo Dragón is involved in geothermal, wind, solar, and natural-gas generation across Mexico. 

Immigration and Gentrification

Immigration was also discussed. Spurred by Max Keiser’s enthusiasm about the country, where he roughly said that the world should recognize El Salvador’s arc and that people — bitcoiners presumably — should migrate; suddenly the topic was set on the table. Ruiz, whose family is from the region but was born and raised in the U.S., moved to El Salvador three years ago and has become a recognizable figure in the local Bitcoin community. He followed up with a question about immigration, in particular about gentrification and possible resentment from the local population towards Western migrants, pointing to very negative online comments about some Bitcoiners, such as being called “colonizers”.

Bukele asked back, “When you go out, walk around, and interact with Salvadorans, what are the interactions like?”, The question, to anyone that’s spent time in El Salvador in recent years, answers itself. Salvadorians are very welcoming, Ruiz told Bitcoin Magazine; “there’s a lot of love. People receive us with open arms, and they’re glad we’re here, and they’re happy”. 

Immigration in El Salvador actually tends to be from regional countries like Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Colombia, with smaller numbers reported from the United States. Bukele went on to dismiss concerns about immigration, joking that you could host the whole population of the world in El Salvador by matching the population density of Manhattan. This was not a statement meant to be taken as a goal or ideal, but rather to set the topic in context. He added that the country is obviously looking for the most capable and intelligent people, and even said that “all great empires were built with immigrants’ help”, which says a lot about the President’s mindset on the topic.

In response to concerns about gentrification, the President told the story of a fisherman and house caretaker who got a raise from $300 to $800 a month from an American who bought the property. As a result, the fisherman was able to buy a motor for his boat, which he used to fish and row by hand before that. The scale-up of his fishing business was so productive that the caretaker even got his son a boat, doubling his fishing fleet. The only people who complained about this growth in wages were the neighbours, so the story goes, who must have been feeling the pressure from their own villa’s caretakers, wanting a raise from meager wages. 

Among other Topics

At some point Efrat asked, “How come you are criticized around the world despite El Salvador’s GDP growth, a strengthening economy and popularity at home, which I saw firsthand talking to locals and visiting some of the areas once worst hit by gang violence?”

“Because I’m not part of their club,” the President allegedly responded, “I’m not the kind of ruler they like”. He added that there are evil people in the world who use mainstream media to criticize leaders like him and “call him names”, central bankers, including the ECB, came up as one of the forces behind the negative media campaign against Bukele.

Beyond the clear hit pieces, he noted that many people in governments or the international political establishment are not evil per se, but are often ‘order followers’, who operate on certain narratives and resist new paradigms. 

The recent wins for the country in terms of education reform were also discussed. Bukele allegedly said that many private schools are now integrating similar AI tutoring programs as the one led by his administration. The results made international news when the pilot program deployed in public schools over the past couple of years brought PISA test results to par with Germany and Switzerland.

Renaissance 2.0

When asked about their reflections on the presidential dinner and the Bitcoin Histórico conference in general, Max Kaiser shared his vision in a manner that merits being printed in full:

“Bitcoin Histórico promised two days of Excellence Only, as the Bitcoin Office likes to say, and it delivered big time. The National Palace was a regal setting to showcase the Renaissance 2.0 taking shape in El Salvador with presentations by the best Bitcoin minds and builders in the world. Audience members felt like they had been transported to a time and place found nowhere else in the world right now, where hope and happiness are in abundance. No doom.”

Stacy Herbert, whose presence and attention to detail were felt throughout the festivities, told Bitcoin Magazine, “We promoted Bitcoin Histórico as an elevated bitcoin conference experience with Philosopher King meets Renaissance 2.0 vibes. In every detail, my team and I achieved that, including with the official Bitcoin Office dinner at Casa Presidencial.” She added that guests were free to ask any question they wanted, and that no topic was off limits. 

“They grilled the President for several hours. His wit, his charm, his intelligence – all unscripted – was there for all to see firsthand. And they will have walked away understanding why it is that El Salvador is winning under his leadership.” Herbert added. As far as attendees to the dinner who Bitcoin Magazine spoke with, both claims remain very much corroborated.

This post Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt.

He added that the country is obviously looking for the most capable and intelligent people, and even said that “all great empires were built with immigrants’ help”, which says a lot about the President’s mindset on the topic.

In response to concerns about gentrification, the President told the story of a fisherman and house caretaker who got a raise from $300 to $800 a month from an American who bought the property. As a result, the fisherman was able to buy a motor for his boat, which he used to fish and row by hand before that. The scale-up of his fishing business was so productive that the caretaker even got his son a boat, doubling his fishing fleet. The only people who complained about this growth in wages were the neighbours, so the story goes, who must have been feeling the pressure from their own villa’s caretakers, wanting a raise from meager wages. 

Among other Topics

At some point Efrat asked, “How come you are criticized around the world despite El Salvador’s GDP growth, a strengthening economy and popularity at home, which I saw firsthand talking to locals and visiting some of the areas once worst hit by gang violence?”

“Because I’m not part of their club,” the President allegedly responded, “I’m not the kind of ruler they like”. He added that there are evil people in the world who use mainstream media to criticize leaders like him and “call him names”, central bankers, including the ECB, came up as one of the forces behind the negative media campaign against Bukele.

Beyond the clear hit pieces, he noted that many people in governments or the international political establishment are not evil per se, but are often ‘order followers’, who operate on certain narratives and resist new paradigms. 

The recent wins for the country in terms of education reform were also discussed. Bukele allegedly said that many private schools are now integrating similar AI tutoring programs as the one led by his administration. The results made international news when the pilot program deployed in public schools over the past couple of years brought PISA test results to par with Germany and Switzerland.

Renaissance 2.0

When asked about their reflections on the presidential dinner and the Bitcoin Histórico conference in general, Max Kaiser shared his vision in a manner that merits being printed in full:

“Bitcoin Histórico promised two days of Excellence Only, as the Bitcoin Office likes to say, and it delivered big time. The National Palace was a regal setting to showcase the Renaissance 2.0 taking shape in El Salvador with presentations by the best Bitcoin minds and builders in the world. Audience members felt like they had been transported to a time and place found nowhere else in the world right now, where hope and happiness are in abundance. No doom.”

Stacy Herbert, whose presence and attention to detail were felt throughout the festivities, told Bitcoin Magazine, “We promoted Bitcoin Histórico as an elevated bitcoin conference experience with Philosopher King meets Renaissance 2.0 vibes. In every detail, my team and I achieved that, including with the official Bitcoin Office dinner at Casa Presidencial.” She added that guests were free to ask any question they wanted, and that no topic was off limits. 

“They grilled the President for several hours. His wit, his charm, his intelligence – all unscripted – was there for all to see firsthand. And they will have walked away understanding why it is that El Salvador is winning under his leadership.” Herbert added. As far as attendees to the dinner who Bitcoin Magazine spoke with, both claims remain very much corroborated.

This post Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt.

title: Bitcoin Price Retests $61,500 – Same Zone It Lost in June
description:
Bitcoin has dropped from near $87,380 to $61,550, cutting through its daily moving averages and Fibonacci supports before landing on […]
The post Bitcoin Price Retests $61,500 – Same Zone It Lost in June appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Bitcoin has dropped from near $87,380 to $61,550, cutting through its daily moving averages and Fibonacci supports before landing on the zone where it turned repeatedly in June and July.

Key Takeaways

  • Price sits on June-July demand near $61,500
  • Daily RSI at 19.93, deep in oversold
  • Price trades 15% below 200-day SMA
  • Thursday’s high stalled just below $64,115

Whether that zone holds again is the main question on the BTCUSDT daily chart, after it gave way once in late June and then held through the summer.

Four Fibonacci Levels Gone in November

The retracement grid runs from the late-June low near $57,780 to the September peak near $87,380. Price slipped under the rising dashed trendline from that low in late October, and the November selloff then ran through four retracement levels in turn.

The 0.382 level near $76,070 went first. The 0.5 retracement near $72,580 followed on heavy red candles, and losing it cost two supports at once: the 200-day simple moving average sits close to $72,690, almost on top of it. The 0.618 level near $69,090 barely slowed the decline. Only the 0.786 level near $64,115 produced a pause, a brief bounce before sellers returned.

The 50-day SMA at $78,230 is rolling over sharply, and the 100-day at $77,760 is flattening just beneath it. With the 200-day at $72,690, price now trades about 15% below the slowest of the three averages.

Where Thursday’s Session Stalled

The session opened at $63,060, already below the 0.786 level near $64,115. It rose to $64,080, about $35 short of that line, then turned lower to $61,430. A close near current prices would mean the level that supported the mid-November bounce has now turned price away from below.

The drop brought Bitcoin to the lower edge of the blue horizontal band between roughly $61,500 and $62,300. The band caught the early-June selloff, gave way in late June, when price fell to near $57,780, and was back above it within days. Through July and into mid-August, it absorbed several pullbacks before the breakout toward $76,000. Thursday’s low dipped under $61,500 but stayed above $61,400.

What Oversold Meant Last Time

Daily RSI (14) reads 19.93, well below its own 28.96 average, which shows how far and how fast price has fallen. A reading this low does not mark a bottom by itself.

Early June offers a test case on this chart. RSI dropped deep into oversold territory then too, and price rebounded briefly before breaking below the blue band to the late-June low. An oversold reading can come before a relief rally or only interrupt a decline. In June, it was the second.

What would change the picture on the daily chart:

If the floor holds

Daily closes inside or above the $61,500 zone, with RSI turning up from 19.93, would leave room for a short-covering bounce toward the 0.786 level near $64,115. A stronger relief move would meet the 0.618 retracement near $69,090.

If $61,400 gives way

A decisive daily close below $61,400 would remove the last horizontal buffer above the range floor, leaving the 1.0 Fibonacci level and late-June low near $57,780 as the next reference.

Trend check: a bounce stays counter-trend until price reclaims the level near $64,115 and then the one near $69,090. Both still sit below the 200-day SMA at $72,690 and the 0.5 level near $72,580.

The $61,500 area carries more weight on a bigger chart. Coindoo’s monthly Bitcoin chart analysis traces it to the 2021 double top and the floor of the 2024 range, with the 0.5 Fibonacci retracement near $63,160 just above it. On that timeframe, the November close relative to $61,500 is also the test that matters.

The levels and scenarios described are based on technical analysis of the daily chart and are not predictions of future price movement. Cryptocurrency markets are highly volatile; always do your own research before making any investment decisions.

fullContent:
Privacy coins are poised to be among the biggest cryptocurrency stories of 2027, driven by growing concerns over financial surveillance, institutional adoption, and the future of digital privacy. This creates a compelling investment narrative. Google Gemini AI predicts that two projects, Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC), will stand out, and it aims to forecast which will experience a significant price surge in 2027.

Both Monero and Zcash are established leaders in the privacy-focused cryptocurrency space, but they employ fundamentally different approaches to protecting users’ financial information. Monero offers privacy by default, while Zcash seeks to balance financial confidentiality with greater accessibility for institutional investors.

As a potential major crypto bull market approaches in 2027, investors may find two distinct opportunities for substantial returns. However, determining which option could deliver the biggest gains may yield surprising results.

Monero vs. Zcash: Two Different Approaches to Privacy

Monero has long been considered the gold standard for transaction privacy. Unlike conventional cryptocurrencies, where transactions can be publicly inspected on a blockchain, XMR makes privacy an inherent feature of its network.

It achieves this through ring signatures, Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT), and stealth addresses, which conceal the sender, transaction amount, and recipient. Importantly, privacy is mandatory, not optional.

This gives Monero a compelling proposition as a digital cash alternative, especially as blockchain analytics grow more sophisticated and financial surveillance expands.

However, that same characteristic creates a significant obstacle: regulatory scrutiny. Exchanges in several jurisdictions have restricted or removed XMR trading, potentially limiting access to a broader pool of investors.

Zcash takes a different approach, using zero-knowledge cryptography to enable shielded transactions while retaining the option of transparent transactions.

Its shielded addresses let users conceal transaction details, while viewing keys let them selectively disclose information to auditors or other authorized parties. This flexibility could prove particularly attractive to institutions that want privacy without completely sacrificing compliance.

The distinction could become increasingly important as institutional investors look beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum for opportunities in specialized crypto sectors.

Gemini AI Predicts a Privacy Boom: Could Institutional Adoption Drive the Next Rally?

Privacy coins are already attracting attention beyond their traditional communities. Zcash has made considerable progress in positioning itself as a more institutionally accessible privacy network, with regulated investment products emerging and interest in its underlying technology growing.

Meanwhile, Monero continues to benefit from its established reputation, consistent privacy guarantees and decentralized architecture.

The broader investment narrative is also changing. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more transactions become visible to blockchain analytics companies, incentivizing individuals and businesses to seek greater financial confidentiality.

However, the regulatory landscape could become a major obstacle in 2027. The EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation is scheduled to apply from July 10, 2027, with restrictions covering crypto-asset accounts involving anonymity-enhancing coins.

Crucially, the legislation’s definition encompasses privacy features that operate either systematically or optionally. This means neither project can assume its architecture provides an exemption.

XMR vs. ZEC: What Does the Long-Term Chart Suggest?

For Monero, the key technical consideration is whether it can establish a sustained higher-high structure following its previous major market cycle. A successful retest of former resistance zones as support could lay the groundwork for another substantial move, particularly if capital rotates toward privacy-focused assets.

XMR also benefits from a relatively predictable supply model. Its permanent tail emission produces 0.6 XMR every two minutes, with an inflation rate that gradually declines over time.

Zcash, meanwhile, has a more conventional fixed supply of 21 million coins, giving it a familiar scarcity narrative. Its longer-term technical outlook will depend heavily on whether it can maintain gains tied to its growing institutional profile and establish stronger historical support.

Both could benefit enormously from a broader cryptocurrency bull market, although ZEC’s previous outperformance means investors should also consider the possibility of profit-taking and deeper corrections.

Which Privacy Coin Could Deliver the Biggest Gains in 2027?

There are compelling arguments for both projects, but their potential price trajectories could look quite different. In an optimistic 2027 scenario, Zcash could target a broad trading range of $1,600–$2,400, supported by institutional demand, increased shielded transaction adoption, and a stronger position within the privacy sector.

Monero could potentially push towards $900–$1,400, with a particularly bullish scenario opening the door to even higher valuations if demand for censorship-resistant digital cash accelerates.

These are speculative price scenarios, not technical guarantees, and regulatory restrictions remain a substantial risk for both projects. Nevertheless, one important consideration could give XMR the advantage: its established position as a dedicated privacy currency.

Zcash arguably has the stronger institutional narrative, but Monero arguably has the stronger proposition for users who consider financial privacy non-negotiable. If that distinction becomes increasingly important during the next market cycle, demand for XMR could accelerate considerably.

Gemini AI Predicts the Top Privacy Coin for 2027: Monero (XMR)

While Zcash could continue attracting institutional capital and potentially deliver impressive returns, I believe Monero has the ingredients for a stronger percentage gain over the longer term.

Its established reputation, mandatory privacy architecture, and potential to benefit from renewed demand for financial anonymity make it an intriguing candidate. If privacy becomes one of crypto’s defining investment narratives in 2027, XMR could be one of the biggest beneficiaries.

title: Coinbase Entered Prediction Markets With Kalshi. Now It Plans to Become a Rival
description:
Coinbase Global Inc. is preparing to shift part of its prediction-market business onto its own infrastructure, to gain direct control over which markets it lists and to retain a larger share of trading revenue. 
The proprietary event contracts for U.S. customers may go live on Coinbase as early as in the first half of 2027, according to a Bloomberg report. 
 From Kalshi Distribution to Proprietary Listings 
Coinbase currently offers prediction markets through a partnership with federally regulated exchange Kalshi. When the company first rolled out the product in December 2025, it said all initial market flow would come through Kalshi’s venue. 
That distribution model has rapidly scaled into a meaningful business line. During its third-quarter earnings update on October 29, Coinbase disclosed that its prediction markets offering had surpassed an annualised revenue run rate of $200 million. 
 At the time, Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas hinted at plans to introduce its own event contracts to improve the product’s unit economics. 
While Bloomberg’s latest report puts a specific first-half 2027 timeframe on that rollout, Coinbase has not yet officially confirmed a launch date.
Assembling the Full Derivatives Stack 
Coinbase has spent the past year assembling the regulatory and technical pieces needed to list and settle event contracts independently. 
The exchange announced an agreement to acquire the Clearing Company, a prediction-markets startup led by Toni Gemayel, in December 2025, soon after the launch of the Kalshi-powered product.
 The next step came on 28th September 2026 when Coinbase Clearing obtained registration from the CFTC as a DCO for fully collateralised contracts. 
 That approval completed a three-part vertical stack under the Coinbase umbrella. Coinbase Financial Markets handles client accounts as the Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), Coinbase Derivatives  lists contracts as the Designated Contract Market (DCM), and Coinbase Clearing settles trades as the DCO. 
The ‘Everything Exchange’ Strategy 
Bringing the event contracts in-house is consistent with the 'Everything Exchange' strategy that Coinbase laid out when it entered the space last year. 
 Rather than treating prediction markets as a bit of a novelty in themselves, they're embedded within the broader interface with crypto, equities and derivatives. It's a case of vertical integration to capture both the retail order flow and the underlying exchange economics.


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: Third-Party JavaScript Is Part of Your Attack Surface: Lessons from a Recent Supply-Chain Attack
description: In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service. […]
fullContent:
In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.

The attackers did not break into those websites. Instead, they exploited a weakness in the vendor’s platform to gain administrative control of some customer accounts, then modified the JavaScript those customers delivered through the vendor. The vendor’s CDN served the altered code to every visitor of an affected page.

Researchers who analyzed the injected code found it running on many organizations’ websites. It was built to steal payment card details typed into on-page forms, tamper with cryptocurrency transactions, and send readable cookies to attacker-controlled servers.

The lesson extends beyond one vendor: modern websites run code their owners did not write and often do not track.

The hidden risk of third-party JavaScript

Analytics, personalization, advertising, consent management, chat, and A/B testing all depend on external scripts. Each <script src> that points to another host lets that host run code in your visitors’ browsers with the same privileges as your own code. It can read and change the page, watch form input, read cookies not marked HttpOnly, and send data out.

That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise. The attack did not require any change to the affected organizations’ source code, servers, or pipelines. The malicious file was served from the vendor’s own CDN, with the vendor’s valid certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted. Code review and server-side monitoring had nothing to catch. One weakness in a shared platform reached many organizations in a single day.

What Content Security Policy can and cannot do

Content Security Policy (CSP) tells the browser which sources may load scripts and receive data. In this incident, the injected code loaded its main payload from an attacker-controlled domain, so a strong CSP could block it.

But much depends on the word strong. Most affected sites had either no CSP or one that still let the payload run. Allowlisting the vendor’s domain made no difference, because the malicious code came through that host. Protection came from a restrictive script-src that did not allow the attacker’s domain. ‘unsafe-eval’ let an inline fallback copy of the payload run, and ‘strict-dynamic’ extended trust to scripts the compromised snippet inserted. A tight connect-src limited exfiltration but could not stop wallet-address swapping inside the page.

Reducing third-party script risk: guidance for every organization

These practices apply to any organization that runs external JavaScript on its website.

  • Know what runs on your pages. Keep an inventory of every third-party script, the pages that load it, who owns it internally, and why it is needed. Include scripts added through tag managers.
  • Load less, especially on sensitive pages. Remove scripts that no longer serve a purpose, and keep analytics, marketing, and testing scripts off payment, login, and account pages unless they are essential.
  • Enforce a strict Content Security Policy. Allow only the script and connection sources each page needs, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’ and ‘unsafe-inline’, use nonces or hashes where you can, and enable violation reporting. Roll out changes in Report-Only mode first.
  • Keep payment entry out of reach. Hosted payment fields, served in an iframe from your payment provider’s domain, cannot be read by scripts running on your own page.
  • Protect cookies and sessions. Mark session and authentication cookies HttpOnly so injected scripts cannot read them, and set Secure and SameSite as well.
  • Pin or self-host what rarely changes. Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for third-party files that change infrequently, or host them yourself. Scripts that change often, such as tag managers and testing tools, need monitoring instead.
  • Hold script vendors to a high standard. Ask providers how they secure customer accounts and code changes, and how quickly they notify customers of incidents. On your own accounts with them, enforce MFA or SSO and limit who can publish code.
  • Watch for changes. Monitor third-party scripts for new code, new network destinations, and unexpected behavior. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.
  • Plan your response. Know how to disable a third-party script quickly, and keep web, CDN, and CSP logs long enough to investigate an incident.

How Qualys TotalAppSec helps identify exposure

1. Assess Content Security Policy: QIDs 150206 and 150207

QID 150206 – Content-Security-Policy Not Implemented flags applications that send no CSP header, which leaves no browser-enforced limit on where scripts can load from.

QID 150207 – Content Security Policy Insecure Configuration flags weak elements: ‘unsafe-inline’, ‘unsafe-eval’, wildcard sources, a missing default-src, and missing or invalid reporting configuration. This incident showed the effect of one of these directly, when ‘unsafe-eval’ let the inline payload run.

A QID 150207 finding does not mean a given policy would have allowed this particular attack. That depends on the full policy, including script-src, trusted sources, and nonces or hashes. Treat these findings as starting points for a policy review. Reporting matters as well. The vendor’s first investigative recommendation was to review CSP violation reports, and sites without reporting had none to review.

2. Discover external JavaScript dependencies: QID 150545

QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL. It does not judge whether a library is malicious. Its value is visibility: an inventory of external scripts is the basis for deciding which vendors to trust and which hosts a CSP should allow.

3. Find applications that serve known malicious scripts 533507 (new)

We have released QID 533507 – Known Malicious Script Reference Detected. This unauthenticated check sends an HTTP GET request and inspects the response body for a script src referencing known malicious scripts.

Use it to inventory which applications load known malicious scripts and to prioritize the applications handling payments or cryptocurrency for CSP review.

Detecting malicious content with Qualys Web Malware Detection

TotalAppSec shows where you are exposed and how well your controls are configured. Qualys Web Malware Detection asks a different question: is malicious content present? Qualys Web Malware Detection combines heuristic analysis (signature rules for patterns such as encoded JavaScript); behavioral analysis (visiting the site with a vulnerable browser and watching for unexpected file writes or processes); reputation checks of pages, referenced URLs, and remotely loaded resources against public blacklists; and antivirus scanning of downloaded scripts and files. Three detections relate directly to third-party script risk:

  • QID 207003 – A Match to a Known Virus was Detected: a file written to disk during page rendering is identified as malicious by a virus scanner.
  • QID 208000 – Content was Loaded from a Remote Malicious Page: a page loads scripts, iframes, or images from a blacklisted domain.
  • QID 208001 – A Link to a Malicious Page was Found: a page links to a domain on one or more blacklists.

Reputation-based detection depends on a domain being blacklisted at scan time. Attacker infrastructure is often new: Report URI found this campaign’s primary domain was registered the morning the attack began. Continuous scanning, alongside preventive controls such as CSP, is paramount for that reason.

Together, these findings give three different views. A script reference (QIDs 533507, 150545) shows where you depend on someone else. A weak control (QIDs 150206, 150207) shows how much damage a compromised dependency could do. Malicious content (QIDs 207003, 208000, 208001) is evidence that something harmful is present.

At a glance: what each detection tells you

Recommendations for security teams

Follow the actions in the vendor’s report. Confirm which pages ran the snippet during the exposure window, review CSP violation reports and outbound requests against the published indicators of compromise, and keep your web, CDN, and CSP logs. The vendor and Report URI published different indicators, so check both.

For every organization:

  1. Inventory third-party scripts. Use QIDs 533507 and 150545 to see which applications load external JavaScript, and from where.
  2. Restrict trusted sources. Remove unneeded scripts, especially from payment, login, and personal-data pages.
  3. Implement CSP and assess it continuously. Resolve QID 150206 and 150207 findings, keep script-src and connect-src restrictive, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’, and test changes in Report-Only mode.
  4. Monitor third-party script changes. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.
  5. Investigate malicious content. Treat Web Malware Detection findings as triggers for investigation.
  6. Remove unauthorized scripts and remediate. Restore known-good code and rotate secrets stored in readable cookies.
  7. Reassess after remediation. Rescan to confirm that fixes are in place.

Conclusion

The incident here did not require breaching a single customer’s application. It required one weakness in a platform those applications trusted. Securing a web application means having visibility into both the code you write and the external scripts you allow to run in your users’ browsers. Qualys TotalAppSec and Web Malware Detection help you inventory those dependencies, check the controls that limit their impact, and find malicious content.
